Under homogeneous tasks and label spaces, similar retention-adaptation behavior is observed across public benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Sachithx/PACT.

authors.name: Sachith Abeywickrama, Peiliang Gong, Emadeldeen Eldele, Min Wu, Chau Yuen

papers.title: Embodied Graph: A Relational World Model for Long-Horizon Tasks
papers.summary: Long-horizon tasks in embodied and web environments involve extended decision sequences and delayed feedback, making accurate planning crucial for success. World models tackle this by learning latent dynamics for imagination-based planning. However, existing approaches merely rely on dense pixel-level observations, which forces the model to absorb redundant information while overlooking relations among task-relevant entities. Consequently, small errors may accumulate over long imagined rollouts and gradually corrupt the predictions. In this paper, we explore world models that imagine over sparse state abstractions, which poses two key challenges: 1) how to remove redundant information and form a compact state abstraction; 2) how to incorporate the relational structure to learn reliable long-horizon dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose Embodied Graph, a relational state abstraction that supports structured dynamics modeling and long-horizon imagination, and the Relational World Model (RWM), which performs imagination directly over graph states. RWM consists of (i) a Task-Aware Embodied Graph Constructor that filters redundant details and maintains graph memory through online updates, and (ii) an Embodied Graph Recurrent State Space Model that learns node-wise latent dynamics while capturing inter-node dependencies. The imagined graph states provide predictions of action consequences to guide decision-making. Experiments on Minecraft and Crafter demonstrate the effectiveness of RWM in embodied environments. Notably, in Minecraft, RWM is the only method that obtains diamonds within the given budget. Experiments on web interaction further illustrate the applicability of relational state prediction to the decision making process of web agents.

authors.name: Zongyuan Wu, Xin Wang, Tongtong Feng, Yuan Meng, Zeyang Zhang, Ling Feng, Wenwu Zhu

papers.title: Fast Bayesian Methods for Uncertainty Quantification in Sparse AI Evaluation
papers.summary: Estimating how an AI system will perform on a new benchmark need not require another large model. We use public evaluation counts to choose a weak Beta prior, then update it exactly from at most 31 revealed outcomes. The predictor uses no item semantics, pretrained weights, or inference API. Its single online evaluation in the AIMS competition returned a team-reported Brier ALC of 0.188477, a 24.6% reduction from the constant-0.5 reference. The complete submission is 7,754 bytes; a server microbenchmark measures 12.71 microseconds per prediction with 31 matching labels. We describe how source evaluations are compressed into 301 prior means and show why a concentration of two lets new evidence rapidly determine the prediction. The resulting posterior gives exact uncertainty about the modelled success rate without numerical integration or neural inference. A public evaluation covers 79 system-benchmark pairs and eight seeds, reaching Brier ALC 0.200250 for the submitted method. Accompanying code and sufficient statistics reconstruct the fitted prior byte for byte and replay all 632 evaluation trajectories. The result demonstrates how much predictive value a compact Bayesian model can extract from sparse target feedback at very low online cost.

authors.name: Dario Deniz Ergun, Haohua Wang, Brendon Tao, Jonah Kollenberg, Chen Ye Gan

papers.title: GALA: Gallery-Level Alignment for Real-Life Vision Decoding from EEG
papers.summary: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.

authors.name: Philippe Forest, Giulia Lioi, Mai Pham Quyen, Alix Lamouroux, Javen Shi, Adrien Merlini

papers.title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming
papers.summary: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.

authors.name: Xiaoyang Xing, Wenyu Dai, Xiaoliang Gong, Asoke K Nandi, Anthony Cohn

papers.title: From Points to Trajectories: Rethinking Multimodal Alignment for Physical Events
papers.summary: Advancing physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) requires moving beyond static object recognition to ground how real-world mechanics (e.g., impact, friction, and force transfer) unfold over time. While multimodal aligners seek to capture these interactions by matching multi-sensor streams, prevailing architectures compress each temporal sequence into a single pooled embedding. We show that this paradigm fails on twin events: distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. Collapsing the temporal dimension averages out transient cross-modal dynamics, effectively reducing physical event alignment to static scene recognition. Formally, we prove that as sequence length increases, any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition. Consequently, as windows grow, no choice of loss function or embedding geometry can disambiguate twin events from pooled features alone. Instead, we show that physical events are uniquely identified by the event gap, namely the instantaneous, synchronous co-fluctuations across modalities that are erased by pooling and accumulate only along unpooled trajectories. To recover this signal, we introduce CounterPoint, a lightweight plug-in module that strips out each modality's temporal mean to score frame-level cross-modal agreement. Integrated across four state-of-the-art (SOTA) multimodal aligners, CounterPoint shifts representations from coarse condition matching to fine-grained physical event alignment, consistently outperforming existing temporal alignment methods.

authors.name: Yiyang Zhu, Guangyuan Liu, Jingdi Lei, Li Wei, Chau Yuen

papers.title: FedE2E: One-Shot Federated Learning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop Evaluation
papers.summary: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. However, existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods mainly focus on perception tasks. To address these limitations, we propose \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving. It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models. Closed-loop evaluation on Bench2Drive demonstrates the effectiveness of \method in both one-shot and multi-round federated learning. In the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85, which is 4.07 points higher than prior work. In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, the best performance among all compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.

authors.name: Tao Lian, Antonio M. L\'opez

papers.title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.

authors.name: Eduardo Reck Miranda, Moein Fahmideh Vatandoost

papers.title: KnowledgeClaw: Towards Agentic Knowledge Engineering via Omnimodal Hypergraphs
papers.summary: Knowledge engineering (KE) turns raw files into a reasoning-ready knowledge base, a task now within reach of LLM agents. KE has progressed from chunk and graph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to memory agents, agentic KE and multimodal KE. However, a live knowledge base needs omnimodality, a closed-loop lifecycle and multi-granular application at once, yet existing systems meet at most two and no benchmark measures all three. We formalize Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE) and release OmniKE-Bench, six tasks with 1,829 model-free items over 3,960 real files in five modalities. We further propose KnowledgeClaw, an agentic system that builds an omnimodal typed hypergraph, keeps it current with a closed-loop lifecycle agent and routes each query to the granularity it needs. Against 30 baselines, it ranks first on all six tasks with an overall OKE of 55.9, +14.6 over the strongest baseline. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/KnowledgeClaw.

authors.name: Haoran Luo, Jiapu Wang, Linhao Luo, Luu Anh Tuan

papers.title: OpenKAGE: Open-Ended Lifelong Learning in the Open World via Knowledge-Sharing Agent-Group Evolution
papers.summary: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.

authors.name: Wenhao Yuan, Longhui Yuan, Zexi Jia, Ningzhe Shi, Jingwei Li, Shipeng Cen, Pengcheng Luo, Jie Zhou, Jinchao Zhang

papers.title: Benchmarking LLM abilities on postdoc-level natural science problems
papers.summary: Scientific problems have no answer key, so evaluating an agent means deciding what counts as a better solution before any agent is run. Existing benchmarks either match a symbolic answer against a key or, where they require executable work, score it by unit tests, by a rubric, or by position on a competition leaderboard. None of these is the criterion by which a field decides that one published method beats another. STEMBench adopts that criterion directly. Each of its twelve research problems in high-energy physics, astrophysics and neuroscience is scored by its own field's figure of merit, and each comes with two measured anchors: a submission that uses no domain knowledge, and an expert reference reproducing a published method, both obtained by running code shipped with the benchmark. The interval between them states how much of a problem is crossed by scientific insight rather than by engineering. Across eight frontier models, task-level wins and domain-level leadership dissociate: a model that wins five of the twelve tasks leads no domain mean. In the high-effort cross-model comparison, at least one model's mean score exceeds the expert anchor on seven of twelve tasks. The remaining five span uncertainty estimation, latent and causal inference, and cross-site clinical classification. Numerical scores and official-submission validity capture different aspects of performance and are reported separately. We release the tasks, graders, anchors and harness.

authors.name: Alina Avanesyan, Alexey Boldyrev, Liqun Deng, Denis Derkach, Mary Godunova, Mikhail Hushchyn, Dmitry Ilvovsky, Irina Knyazeva, Irina Piontkovskaya, Dmitry Polubotko, Fedor Ratnikov, Ekaterina Trofimova, Zhenhe Zhang

papers.title: Reducing Inference Cost of Coding Agents with Timeout Cascades
papers.summary: AI coding agents have become one of the most popular applications of large language models. Yet, agentic AI comes at the cost of a tremendous amount of GPU compute resources, which limits its profitability and its viability at scale. In this paper, we investigate whether smaller, cheaper models can cut this cost without sacrificing accuracy. We evaluate 36 popular large and small open-weight models released since 2024 on a software engineering benchmark, and find that recent small models are closing the accuracy gap compared to their large counterparts. We investigate the structure of this gap and find that the gap is highly concentrated around hard tasks that small language models fail to solve while achieving remarkably good accuracy for easy and medium complexity tasks. Following this observation, we show that by utilizing a hybrid inference strategy that tries a small model first and escalates to a large one only when needed, we can achieve up to 33% reduction in total GPU-hour costs and 16.4% on all tasks from SWE-bench Verified, without sacrificing accuracy. Strikingly, this simple cascade nearly matches an oracle-style task router, highlighting a practical path for deploying cost-aware coding agents in production without complex learned task routers and with minimal engineering complexity.

authors.name: Boxi Zhou, German Sviridov, Dmitrii Ustiugov, Haris Javaid

papers.title: automodel: A Skill for Agentic Model Discovery
papers.summary: The search for better models, whether expressed as analytical equations or neural architectures, has increasingly shifted from manual design toward data-driven automation. While a multitude of algorithms exist, ranging from exhaustive search to AlphaEvolve, recent advances in general-purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex raise the question: could providing such systems with a "model discovery recipe" be enough to discover or improve models? We present automodel, an agent skill for general model discovery. With case studies in astrophysics, cardiovascular dynamics, precision agriculture, traffic flow, and vehicle tire dynamics, we show how commercial agents equipped with automodel can successfully identify novel and scientifically-relevant models. Our findings suggest that encoding model-discovery methodology as a portable agent skill can provide a simple, interactive, powerful and broadly applicable alternative to domain-specific automated discovery pipelines. The skill is available at: https://github.com/unlayer-ai/automodel.

authors.name: Marco Virgolin, Harry Desmond, Ester Bergantin, Giorgio Morales, John W. Sheppard, Luigi Romano, Alessandro Lucantonio

papers.title: When Figures Disagree with Text: Evaluating Autonomous Visual Evidence Verification in Scientific Papers
papers.summary: Scientific figures carry evidence for the claims that cite them, so reviewing a paper means checking that a figure agrees with the text, and not only describing what the figure shows. Benchmarks of figure-text verification typically hand the model the figure, the claim, or the knowledge that an inconsistency exists, which leaves untested whether a model can find the figure worth checking in a complete paper, relate a visual element to the claim it conflicts with, and recognize the conflict. We study this autonomous setting on 31 full manuscripts, each carrying a reviewer-documented figure-text inconsistency from PRISMM-Bench that is hidden from the model. Six multimodal models review each PDF under a neutral prompt, and we then add one input at a time to the same manuscripts. Of 1,445 open-ended reviews, 60.6% mention the flawed figure, yet a grading rubric accepts only 3.3% as diagnosing its contradiction; a blind audit finds the rubric lenient, so we read these as rubric-accepted rates and compare conditions rather than absolute values. In a separate controlled run, naming the figure, without stating that it is flawed, raises rubric-accepted diagnosis from 4.3% to 20.4%, while a consistency instruction and coarse visual cues do not. When the contradiction is visible only in the rendered figure, text-only review yields no accepted diagnosis, while review of the rendered pages with the figure named reaches 15.8%. A baseline that lets the model choose which figures to check, ranked by centrality, stays at 4.8%. Deciding what to verify is thus a large part of the difficulty, and the selection rule we tested does not resolve it. Multimodal document understanding should be evaluated on whether a model can propose what to verify, not only answer questions about a figure it is handed.

authors.name: Guijia Zhang, Hongbo Qiu, Jiajun Zha, Guohao Cai, Hao Zheng, Huihao Jing, Kexu Cheng, Shipeng Luo, JinYang Huang, Shing-Chi Cheung, Changsheng Lu, Haoxuan Che, Harry Yang

papers.title: Semantic Context Handoff with On-Demand Evidence for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.summary: Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. As execution proceeds, this history keeps growing, increasing inference cost and potentially degrading accuracy. Existing methods control this growth by preserving compact conclusions while removing earlier observations, but doing so can discard evidence that later becomes relevant. We introduce Semantic Context Handoff (SCH), whose central abstraction is state--evidence separation: a compact semantic state carries the agent's current interpretation, while supporting action--observation evidence remains separately addressable and can re-enter context when later execution makes it relevant, without separate summarization or retrieval-model calls. Empirically, SCH improves long-horizon agent performance while substantially reducing context cost. In a controlled 150-task SWE-bench study, SCH's evidence recovery improves Pass@1 from $80.0\%$ to $86.9\%$ at essentially unchanged token use and execution time. In the complete-system comparison, SCH achieves 86.9% Pass@1 while using 43% fewer tokens and 41% less wall-clock time than the strongest baseline by task performance. Across models and benchmarks, SCH consistently reduces token use relative to full-history prompting while remaining competitive with or improving upon the evaluated baselines. Trajectory analysis confirms that SCH recovers evidence from substantially earlier parts of the interaction history rather than merely preserving a recent context window.

authors.name: Guolong Zheng, Chen Hou, Xu Yang, Jianshan Zhang, Tao Huang

papers.title: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs
papers.summary: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.

authors.name: Vedant Navale

papers.title: CaDO: Formal Verification-Guided Multi-Agent Framework for Causal Dataset Repair and Generation
papers.summary: High-quality causal reasoning datasets are essential for developing models with reliable causal understanding, particularly in specialized domains. However, existing datasets frequently suffer from incorrect annotations and structural imbalances, which can lead to biased predictions and limited generalization. To address this issue, we propose CaDO (Causal-Engine-Guided Multi-Agent Data Optimization), a multi-agent framework for automated diagnosis and repair of causal reasoning datasets. Our framework consists of three key stages: formal causal reasoning, multi-level diagnosis, and automated data repair and generation. First, a Formalizer Agent translates natural language questions into formal causal queries to minimize semantic deviations and make retrieval and verification more explicit and tractable. Second, a dual-level diagnosis mechanism employs independent Critic Agents to identify sample-level errors while analyzing query-type coverage and label distributions to detect dataset-level structural imbalances. Finally, the framework employs reusable repair operators grounded in formal causal semantics to correct erroneous samples, while Explorer and Expander Agent collaboratively produce diverse and semantically consistent new samples. Experimental results show that CaDO significantly outperforms the strongest of five data cleaning baselines in 16 out of 18 experimental settings, improving downstream model accuracy by up to 9.1%. Moreover, at least 95% of the samples flagged by CaDO are defective, and on CLadder, CaDO incorrectly modifies 92.2% fewer correct labels than an LLM-based judge, demonstrating its effectiveness and reliability. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/thisissyu/cado.

authors.name: Songli Yu, Qi Luo

papers.title: Risk-Triggered Search: Behavior-Preserving Safe Control
papers.summary: Pre-trained visual world models generate multi-step action plans from current and goal observations, yet terminal-proximity objectives fail to prevent forbidden-zone traversal or rigid-body collision sliding. Purely visual interfaces may lack analytical dynamics, structured states, or explicit collision geometry, requiring internal prediction of action-conditioned process risk. We propose Risk-Triggered Search (RTS) for frozen Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world models. Rather than relying on static state features that cannot distinguish candidate plans sharing an observation, RTS unrolls action-conditioned future latent prefixes in the frozen world model and trains a lightweight risk head with process-violation supervision. To intervene selectively while preserving safe nominal behavior, RTS uses the same predicted prefix-risk criterion as both the search trigger gate and hard feasibility gate: safe nominal plans execute directly, whereas alarms trigger local Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) search to minimize nominal deviation within the feasible set. To prevent isotropic Euclidean minimal modification from shrinking obstacle-directed actions into zero-amplitude stalling, we introduce an amplitude-preserving metric $d_{\mathrm{AP}}$ that retains tangential progression while maintaining a unique zero at the nominal plan. Under unified gating and this unique-zero condition, bypassing safe-state search yields closed-loop trajectories strictly identical to every-step same-kernel search. Evaluated under a process-safety benchmark and Safe Arrival Rate (SAR) metric across five tasks, RTS improves SAR over Direct by 12.67--41.67 percentage points on navigation and articulated control and +2.08/+4.17 pp on Cube/PushT boundary cohorts, maintaining 100% action identity with every-step search while cutting controller time by 17.71%--70.41% across 1,968 paired trajectories.

authors.name: Xinyu Deng, Bohao Lan, Kunpeng Li, Mingkai Yuan, Weihang Pan, Binbin Lin

papers.title: Resolution as Attention for Efficient Agent Memory Perception
papers.summary: LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA), a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent's upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent's decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.

authors.name: Siqi Xiang, Zhipeng Xu, Shengrui Liu, Zulong Chen, Chunyan Miao, Shijian Lu

papers.title: From real to synthetic: PSG-GAN learns sleep apnea signal dynamics for AI training
papers.summary: Synthetic polysomnography (PSG) data has great potential in healthcare applications, for example in substituting real data that is sensitive and challenging to collect. Previous research on synthetic PSG data has been largely focused on short segments of individual signals, overlooking the inter-signal dynamics related to sleep disorders. In this study, we developed a generative adversarial network (PSG-GAN) for co-synthesizing longer segments of multiple PSG signals with diverse and complex characteristics typical of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The synthetic signals appeared realistic, and the electroencephalography and electrooculography band powers were similarly distributed across sleep stages. Moreover, the PSG-GAN learned to mirror signal interactions such as changes in photoplethysmography-based heart rate during and after breathing obstructions. An automatic scoring model trained solely with automatically scored synthetic signals reached good performance on sleep staging (\k{appa}=0.71 and 0.63) and respiratory event segmentation (\k{appa}=0.57 and 0.60), on two test sets consisting of healthy volunteers and OSA patients, respectively. This demonstrates the potential of synthetic data in supporting algorithm development for sleep diagnostics. The source code is available at https://github.com/rikuhuttunen/psg-gan.

authors.name: Riku Huttunen, Samu Kainulainen, Matias Rusanen, Sami Myllymaa, Juha T\"oyr\"as, Timo Lepp\"anen, Henri Korkalainen

papers.title: Study and Improvement of Search Algorithms in Stochastic Perfect-Information
papers.summary: In this article, we generalize Unbounded Minimax, the state- of-the-art search algorithm for deterministic zero-sum two- player games with perfect information to the framework of stochastic zero-sum two-player games with perfect informa- tion. We experimentally show that this generalized algorithm achieves better performance than the main stochastic search algorithms.

authors.name: Quentin Cohen-Solal, Tristan Cazenave

papers.title: The Largest Tractable Subclass of Multi-Scale Allen Temporal Reasoning
papers.summary: In this paper, we propose a novel model for temporal reasoning over multi-scale intervals. We show that this model yields a complete reasoning framework and exhibits other particularly interesting properties. Furthermore, we identify the maximal tractable subalgebra for this model, as well as for the other complete model, in the qualitative scales context, which exhibits weaker properties but whose results can be derived by transfer from our new model.

authors.name: Quentin Cohen-Solal

papers.title: ABSClaw: From Invented Worlds to Reality-Grounded Social Simulation
papers.summary: LLM-based artificial societies exhibit rich behavior but often lack scientific grounding: personas and environments are assumed, interaction networks are synthetic, and simulators are generated as free-form code, making results difficult to tie to real populations and sensitive to the backbone model. We argue that simulated worlds should be sampled from observed data, while simulation logic should be implemented by composing operations from a shared, task-independent vocabulary. In this paper, we introduce ABSClaw, a zero-code agent that compiles natural-language requests into executable, reality-grounded social simulations. ABSClaw grounds who acts, where they act, and with whom they interact in survey and census data, geospatial sources, and real networks. It expresses state transitions through 26 atomic operations. To support an open and extensible ecosystem, ABSClaw further allows capabilities to be added as lifecycle-scoped skills without modifying its core. Furthermore, we propose ABSBench, a benchmark of 193 real-world social-simulation tasks. On ABSBench, ABSClaw achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated social simulators. Three real-world case studies show that grounding personas, environments, and interaction networks each improves agreement with observed outcomes. With one runtime skill, ABSClaw executes 13 population-scale simulations, collectively involving 25 million agents. Together, these results demonstrate ABSClaw's real-world fidelity, extensibility, and scalability.

authors.name: Shaobin He, Yan Gao, Quan Zheng, Zhenyang Lin, Zhen Liu, Jiyan He, Shuxin Zheng

papers.title: NaviGATE: Noise-Aware Dual-View Generation for Multimodal Knowledge Graph Reasoning
papers.summary: Multimodal knowledge graph reasoning (MKGR) aims to infer missing facts by jointly exploiting relational structures, textual descriptions, and visual evidence. Existing embedding-based methods effectively capture graph topology, but their fixed multimodal representations are less effective for query-specific fine-grained semantic reasoning, while generation-based methods are vulnerable to noisy retrieval and may produce invalid entities. To address these challenges, we propose NaviGATE, a noise-aware generative framework for MKGR. NaviGATE first aligns graph-derived structural representations with textual semantics, then performs structure-aware internal knowledge activation by fine-tuning the multimodal language model with multimodal entity summaries and injected structural tokens. In the noise-aware dual-view instruction tuning stage, NaviGATE jointly optimizes retrieval-free and retrieval-aware views: reliable retrieved candidates are reinforced through contrastive logit sharpening, while misleading candidates are suppressed through parametric consistency distillation. In inference, structure-constrained decoding restricts generation to valid entities in the target knowledge graph. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that NaviGATE consistently outperforms strong unimodal, multimodal, and generation-based baselines, and remains robust under noisy retrieval scenarios.

authors.name: Jie Peng, Yongxue Shan, Yongfu Zha, Cui Miao, Xiaodong Wang

papers.title: AGAMOTTO: An AI-Enabled Framework for Time-Critical Tactical Course-of-Action Evaluation and Generation
papers.summary: Current command and control (C2) platforms lack integrated simulation capabilities that would allow commanders to dynamically explore courses of action (COAs) during live operations. This paper presents ongoing research and contributions to the development of AGAMOTTO (Advanced Guidance and Analytics for Military Operations, Tactical Threats, and Outcomes) as part of the overarching NGC2 program, which advances the Army's efforts to modernize C2 systems, such as the Tactical Assault Kit (TAK). The paper outlines the current design, preliminary findings, and the remaining research tasks, with an emphasis on how the completed work will support tactical decision-making in future time-constrained environments. While the full system is still under development, initial development and results demonstrate the feasibility of AGAMOTTO. Early experiments highlight both the potential benefits and practical constraints of deploying AI-enabled tools in operational settings, and introduce lessons learned and a viable training strategy to make AI-generated COAs feasible in tactical scenarios.

authors.name: Matthew L. Corbett

papers.title: Think Offline, Act in Real Time: Self-Improving Visual Game Agents through Code
papers.summary: Pre-trained models can read screens and reason about games, yet on an unfamiliar game, an agent still has to learn to play. We ask how an agent can self-improve on such a game from a few of its own attempts, in real-time visual games where the agent sees only the screen and the game keeps running while the agent thinks. We study two kinds of policy that can carry this improvement. In model as policy, a model selects actions during play; we adapt real-time chunking so that committed actions keep executing while the model reasons, and train a 2B controller for this interface. In code as policy, a model writes, tests, and revises a program between attempts, and the program acts during play. Across 170 GameWorld tasks, with at most eight one-minute executions per run, code as policy reaches 47.80% mean progress, against 30.90% for our trained controller, and leads in all five game categories. Improving the controller's weights on a single game, by contrast, yields only modest gains. These results favor letting a model think offline and storing what it learns in a program that acts in real time. Project repository: https://github.com/TabibitoQZP/SIGame

authors.name: Zipeng Qiu, Shusheng Xu, Jiale Li, Yukun Zhou, Chenyue Li, Wenshuang Li, Tongkai Yang, Binhang Yuan

papers.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
papers.summary: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.

authors.name: Firas Spanioli, Yaniv David

papers.title: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
papers.summary: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference labels.We apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2,000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content.We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.

authors.name: Prakhar Mishra, Bhavya Yajush Awasthi, Tanuja, Nishant

papers.title: Movie2Game-Bench: Holistic Evaluation of Film-to-Game Adaptation Beyond Playability
papers.summary: Adapting a film into a game requires selecting source elements and translating them into player actions, rules, and feedback. We introduce Movie2Game-Bench (M2G-bench), a benchmark for evaluating film-to-game adaptation beyond playability. M2G-bench combines general evaluation, movie-specific evaluation, and playtesting by three GUI model players. The protocol connects source content to gameplay steps and implementation evidence, capturing both content preservation and interactive realization. The benchmark comprises 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items. Evaluating 14 models on the same films with their selected primary harnesses reveals complementary strengths in game quality, adaptation, and player experience. A shared weakness concerns playable sequences: this category has the lowest content-presence mean in all 14 models, averaging 37.9 out of 100 compared with 54.8 for iconic elements. Among judgments of retained emotionaldevelopment content, narrative choices account for 60.0% and scenario operation for 7.2%. These findings identify two linked priorities for film-to-game adaptation: preserving source situations that can support gameplay and connecting retained content to player actions and consequences.

authors.name: Jialing Xie, Yifan Zhou, Yiwen Zhang, Junjun He

papers.title: Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.

authors.name: Siyuan Du, Yuxin Liu, Meng Tang, Haoran Li, Yechao Bai, Feiyang Pan, Jia He

papers.title: F$^3$: What Makes Good Experience in World-Action Models?
papers.summary: Deployed world-action models (WAMs) can keep improving only if they make good use of their own experience. Existing methods supply retrieved rollouts or demonstrations to the policy as context, yet such experience often turns previously solved tasks into failures. What, then, makes good experience for a WAM? We show that experience is valuable only in use: its value depends not on whether the source rollout succeeded but on what is stored, when it is used, and where it enters the policy. We therefore propose F$^3$, which makes these three decisions with Form, Fit, and Fusion. Form compresses successful and failed rollouts alike into short, verified operation records; Fit teaches the policy to read a record and to predict when it helps; Fusion injects the record's images, text and actions into the policy as a prefix and an action prior. Trained once on only 200 examples and deployed with a growing experience library, the model achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab without any training on RoboLab: over native Cosmos 3 Nano, it raises success by 12.0 pp and 10.8 pp, reduces steps to success by 12.2% and 11.3%, and cuts regressions by 57%.

authors.name: Zihe Huang, Sirui Zhou, Haozhi Han, Ruge Zhang, Teng Ma, Tao Ma, Zheng Liu, Ce Zhang, Ting Cao, Yunxin Liu, Yunquan Zhang, Yifeng Chen, Kun Li

papers.title: Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading
papers.summary: Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.

authors.name: Haozhe Wu, Zhonghang Li, Chao Huang

papers.title: Choosing What to Observe: Budget-Paired Counterfactual Audits for Credible Evaluation of Visual Agents
papers.summary: Visual agents that read dense documents must ration a finite observation budget across candidate regions, yet answer accuracy conflates where an agent looks, how it adapts to the reads that remain, and how it an?swers once observation stops. We introduce budget-paired counterfactual audits, an evaluation protocol that holds public evidence and region bindings fixed while perturbing only the remaining budget or de?clared task parameters, and credits every acquired history with exact continuation values. The resulting accounting decomposes lost expected accuracy into stepwise acquisition loss and terminal decision loss, separating planning from fixed-role heuristics. Across forty paired routing anchors, five open-weight

authors.name: Ruiqi Liu, Jinming Li, Mo Wang, Yang Lu, Yanlan Kang

papers.title: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules
papers.summary: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

authors.name: Mingliang Zhai, Chuanhao Li, Jiaming Tan, Zhen Li, Yuwei Wu, Yunde Jia, Zian Meng, Yuanyang Yin, Kaipeng Zhang

papers.title: Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs
papers.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves.

authors.name: Yuzhuo Li, Pasan Gunawardena, Yunwei Li

papers.title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems
papers.summary: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.

authors.name: Priyanka Sinha, Sugam Pandey

papers.title: Goemans's Unsplittable-Flow Conjecture: The Anatomy of AI-Assisted Counterexample Discovery
papers.summary: Goemans conjectured that any fractional single-source flow could be converted into an unsplittable flow without increasing total cost and while increasing any arc load by at most the largest demand. Recently, Dmitry Rybin announced a seven-vertex counterexample found through an interaction with ChatGPT, which disproved this long-standing conjecture. However, the interaction did not reveal why this particular topology and its demand, fractional-flow, and cost choices work together, whether the example belongs to a broader family, or which structural features determine where counterexamples can occur. It also left unclear why the AI-assisted search succeeded where earlier human efforts had not. In this paper, we develop a forward counterexample construction pipeline. It starts from an arborescence on which failure is impossible and adds terminal-entering shortcut arcs. The resulting load constraints define a finite set of admissible route choices; their convex hull, the conflict polytope, yields exact conditions for demands, fractional flows, and costs. Starting from a simple arborescence, the pipeline selects Rybin's topology and characterizes all counterexamples it supports. Experiments further demonstrate the pipeline's transferability: when instructed to follow it while varying the initial arborescence and shortcut placement, ChatGPT produced counterexamples on topologies genuinely different from Rybin's and found valid constructions starting from 93 other rooted arborescence shapes. The theory also explains why the original example was difficult to discover through blind enumeration and suggests that Rybin's interaction lies between blind enumeration and a complete theory-guided construction.

authors.name: Jingwei Ge, Na Xie, Li Li, Jiayang Li

papers.title: Response-Relevant Information Is Not Sufficient for Neural Training-State Equivalence
papers.summary: Response-relevant information is not sufficient evidence that two neural networks are in the same training state. We define training-state equivalence operationally: two checkpoints are equivalent, relative to an intervention family and horizon, if they respond alike when training is perturbed and continues. On fresh runs of a one-layer transformer learning modular addition, response to a weight-decay pulse is highly reproducible relative to between-checkpoint differences (rho_state = 0.934 at 500 steps), establishing the target as measurable. Fifteen descriptors of weight spectra, representation geometry and optimiser geometry carry within-run response-relevant information beyond weight norm and loss on a development dataset, predicting held-out response deviation across seed blocks. But their apparent 16.1% advantage at matching checkpoints by future response does not separate from a conditional placebo preserving each descriptor's fitted dependence on the conventional observables, and a calibrated positive control makes simple insensitivity an unlikely explanation. Information a decoder can extract need not be organised in the pairwise geometry that similarity judgments require.

authors.name: Truong Xuan Khanh

papers.title: The Obsolescence of High-Level Code: Agentic Generation from Semantic Artifacts
papers.summary: This paper argues that high-level source code need not remain the primary persistent artifact of software development when AI agents can generate, validate, and regenerate executable implementations from semantic intent. We place this claim in historical context by revisiting application generators, CASE tools, model-driven development, and platforms such as GeneXus, where developers already maintained higher-level representations from which code and other artifacts were derived. We propose a unifying view in which generation is the fundamental operation: given a semantic specification S = (R, C, I, T, O), maintained as the semantic authority, an agent produces a generated executable artifact A. Functional requirements, contracts, and interfaces are assessed as semantic obligations, while tests and operational objectives are assessed by an explicit external oracle V(A, S). We operationalize this framework through an experiment in independent generation: multiple LLVM artifacts are generated directly from one frozen semantic authority and evaluated by the same external oracle. The experiment reports regeneration coherence on an evaluated domain, not a proof of absolute correctness. It provides initial evidence that independently generated executable artifacts can produce the same observable outcomes under a common semantic authority and external oracle. We conclude by discussing reproducibility, specification-centered evolution, and the implications of treating implementation representation as a deployment choice rather than the primary maintained artifact.

authors.name: Di Santi Eduardo

papers.title: What Moves the Ceiling on Automated Audit: from General Code to Scientific Code, Results and Data
papers.summary: Models increasingly check what other models write. We study one shipped arrangement, in which an auditor from a different vendor reads the work and deterministic checks verify what code can verify, and measure its limits against ground truth no model supplies. On general-purpose code with hidden tests, eight readings of the auditor reach 30.0% recall [20.0, 40.7] at 16.0% [10.1, 22.3] flags on correct code, with diminishing returns and no plateau. The reading model (confounded with its sampling), one rulebook sentence and the decision rule each move that figure, and much of what is missed is, on a post hoc rating, behaviour the specification never determined. In three preregistered science studies, checking that reported numbers trace to their sources flagged all 49 inconsistent reports and none of 25 consistent fabrications, of which the model auditor flagged 23 (21 with a sound finding, post hoc); on data, a documentation-derived validator and the auditor flagged overlapping but different faulty items, together 112 of 140 at a 2.9% [0.7, 5.7] flag rate on clean data; and on scientific code, reframing the task around one step cut flags on correct code from 68.7% to 36.0%. Where both tiers ran, the deterministic one flagged no clean item and could not see consistent error; the model saw some and erred itself. Studies making model calls were preregistered, the two unregistered analyses are named, and every quoted report passed independent cross-vendor review.

authors.name: Zhaohe Dong

papers.title: From Data Quality to Data Trustworthiness in AI-Driven Software-Intensive Embedded Systems: A Systematic Review
papers.summary: AI-driven software-intensive embedded systems (SIES) depend on data during development and operation. Poor data quality (DQ) may weaken data trustworthiness, yet evidence about its effects and lifecycle management remains fragmented. This systematic literature review synthesizes 27 primary studies published from January 2020 to February 2026. It examines DQ concerns and evidence linking them to reduced data trustworthiness, along with assessment and management methods. The review identifies 16 concerns organized as Source Quality and Content Quality. Studies provide DQ-based scores and evidence of effects on model or decision performance. Synthesis suggests upstream source or handling problems may become embedded in training baselines and remain difficult to detect at runtime. Eight method categories were identified. Runtime monitoring is the largest category, while upstream and training-time controls remain poorly integrated with runtime assurance. No study covers the full lifecycle. Data trustworthiness supports reliable SIES decisions but is one component of AI-system trustworthiness.

authors.name: Hariharan Gopinath, Jan Bosch, Helena Holmstr\"om Olsson

papers.title: Measuring What Matters in the Age of AI: The Research Software Metrics Landscape
papers.summary: Research software now serves as a primary instrument of science, but the methods the community uses to judge its quality, sustainability, reuse, and impact remain scattered across software engineering, open science, FAIR software, citation, and research-assessment literature. AI-assisted development sharpens the problem: code can be produced at rates that outpace human review capacity, provenance and attribution are harder to track, scholarly credit systems cannot keep pace, and existing metrics inherit assumptions about how research software gets developed that may no longer apply. To aid in navigating these challenges, we present a focused landscape synthesis of research software metrics based on 49 substantive references, organizing the recurring metrics into eight families described by data source, claimed construct, evidence of validity, automation potential, and susceptibility to misuse. Many widely cited research software metrics serve as partial signals but make weak standalone measures of scientific impact. The AI era opens or widens gaps around provenance, maintainability of generated code, reviewer effort, model and data dependencies, reuse and community-health signal inflation, and credit for human labor that AI does not perform. We argue for responsible, contextual, mixed-method use of research software metrics, and offer decision guidance for Research Software Engineers (RSEs), principal investigators, institutions, and funders selecting metrics that support better software, fairer credit, and more trustworthy science. All findings rest on the 49-reference focused review; a reproducible search-and-triage protocol and a 727-record triaged corpus accompany the paper as a transparency artifact for a future full systematic mapping study.

authors.name: Addi Malviya-Thakur, Reed Milewicz, Gregory R. Watson, Audris Mockus

papers.title: Generative AI in Software Testing: Practitioners' Perspectives on the Benefits, Challenges, Opportunities, and Risks
papers.summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) increasingly supports software testing, yet empirical evidence on practitioners' perceptions remains limited. This study investigates perceived benefits, challenges, opportunities, and risks of GenAI in software testing through a questionnaire survey of 64 practitioners. Closed-ended responses were analyzed descriptively, while open-ended responses were qualitatively coded to contextualize the findings. Among the respondents, 34 were users (those with regular or experimental use of GenAI in testing) and 30 were non-users (those without prior use of GenAI in testing). Results show generally positive perceptions of GenAI for reducing effort, test generation, and debugging, alongside concerns about prompt dependence, trust, and incorrect outputs. Users were more positive about several concrete benefits while also more frequently prioritizing reliability-related risks, whereas non-users showed greater uncertainty about some technically specific challenges. Overall, the findings position GenAI as an assistive technology requiring human validation and highlight the importance of considering practitioners' experience with GenAI when interpreting perceptions of GenAI-assisted testing.

authors.name: Chamari Dasanayake, Rahul Mohanani, Vladimir Mandi\'c, Burak Turhan

papers.title: StatePortal: Agentic Checkpoint Synthesis for Testing Deep States in Interactive Software
papers.summary: Large language models have reduced the effort to generate code for interactive software with graphical user interfaces (GUIs). For such software, a key testing bottleneck is reaching a deep state, one that requires a long interaction history. The cost of reaching it recurs across commits, and the GUI automation that could amortize it assumes a DOM or accessibility tree that self-rendered engines do not expose. We introduce StatePortal, an agent that synthesizes a checkpoint, an artifact that restores that state and can be versioned and replayed, from a natural-language functional test case and read-only access to the target's source code. The checkpoint is restored through a per-application hook that an onboarding agent binds or synthesizes once without hand-written hook code. Because a checkpoint can satisfy state checks while rendering incorrectly, checkpoints are scored by hybrid programmatic-state and visual evaluation: acceptance requires both a programmatic-state oracle and a visual oracle to pass. We calibrate the visual oracle against a blinded cross-VLM reference. We release DeepStateBench, 61 deep-state tasks across 10 interactive applications that span five language families and six rendering stacks, with source sizes from 874 to 7.2M lines. Across three registered models, a GUI agent seeded with synthesized checkpoints completes 10.4% of trials, compared with 0% without seeding under the same pixel action space, while StatePortal, which also delivers the target action through the hook, completes 27.5%. Over 1,361 replays of 112 checkpoints, 98.90% reproduce the original verdict with zero model calls, and the hybrid oracle detects 96.25% (77/80) of controlled visual faults invisible to programmatic-state checks alone. We open-source our code at https://github.com/pzy2000/State_Portal and website at https://stateportal.mineyosemite.chatgpt.site

authors.name: Zhiyuan Peng (Shanghai Jiao Tong University), Wei Tao (LIGHTSPEED), Chenhao Ying (Shanghai Jiao Tong University), Yuan Luo (Shanghai Jiao Tong University), Yiwen Guo (Independent Researcher)

papers.title: EnvAgent: Multi-Agent Approach to Building Science Environments in the Clouds
papers.summary: AI agents are transforming scientific computing and software workflows, but generating and executing code requires a correctly configured execution environment. Automating environment construction remains difficult because repositories encode heterogeneous, often incomplete requirements for operating systems, toolchains, dependencies, and build procedures. Existing workflows thus rely on developer-maintained Dockerfiles and setup scripts, making preparation labor-intensive, hard to scale, and potentially biasing evaluations. We present ENVAGENT, an agentic framework that synthesizes, builds, and verifies repository-level Docker environments. ENVAGENT combines deterministic utilities for Docker execution and state management with coordinated agents for repository analysis, planning, Dockerfile synthesis, and iterative failure diagnosis and repair. We also introduce ENVBENCH, a benchmark of 54 scientific artifacts and open-source repositories spanning seven languages from Chameleon Trovi and Multi-SWE-bench. For each repository, we curate a declarative rubric of required structure, configuration, and functionality, and a shared evaluator applies 2,108 weighted checks across generated environments. Across four matched language-model settings, ENVAGENT constructs 43.5 executable environments out of 54 on average, versus 23.5 for Codex and Claude Code, and scores 62.02 versus 24.19 on a composite of executability and rubric satisfaction. These results show that environment-specific agent orchestration substantially improves automated environment construction.

authors.name: Yiming Cheng, Chris Low, Binrui Huang, Mengshi Zhang, Zihao Chen, Kate Keahey, Paul Marshall, Kexin Pei

papers.title: Ephyra: A Property-Based Testing Framework for the LLM Era
papers.summary: Coding agents now write a growing share of software tests; however, property-based testing (PBT) libraries are designed with historical considerations. We present Ephyra, a PBT library in Rust built on three concepts: customizability, observability and generator synthesis. Ephyra lets users compose their own testing loops from generation, mutation and shrinking, and synthesize these components to satisfy functional predicates. Applying Ephyra to 14 open source systems, we have found 349 bugs and reported 300 of them, in database management systems (SQLite, Turso, PostgreSQL, DuckDB, DataFusion), the verified policy engine (Cedar), the SQL equivalence prover (QED), the URL parser used in Node.js (ada-url), reimplementations of existing open source systems in Rust (coreutils, brush, gitoxide), and compilers (binaryen, OCaml, and OxCaml).

authors.name: Alperen Keles

papers.title: When Single Agent Is Enough: Rethinking Multi-Agent Systems for Automated Code Review
papers.summary: Code review plays a critical role in identifying software quality issues and ensuring system robustness. Prior work has proposed techniques for Review Comment Generation (RCG) and Code Refinement (CR), with recent Multi-Agent (MA) approaches achieving state-of-the-art results by coordinating agents specialized in different quality dimensions. However, MA systems introduce substantial architectural complexity and runtime overhead, and recent evidence suggests they may underperform Single-Agent (SA) approaches in certain tasks. In this work, we systematically compare MA and SA designs for RCG and CR. Surprisingly, our results show that SA approaches perform comparably to- and sometimes outperform-MA systems, despite their simpler design. These findings challenge the prevailing assumption that MA architectures are the default choice for complex software engineering tasks.

authors.name: Jiawei Li, Hoa Khanh Dam, Iftekhar Ahmed

papers.title: The Illusion of Relief: How GenAI Redistributes Cognitive Workload in Software Organizations
papers.summary: This study explores how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes software practitioners' cognitive work across software development activities. We analyzed questionnaire responses from 44 practitioners across nine organizations using descriptive quantitative methods and qualitative analysis of relevant open-ended responses. Practitioners reported productivity and time savings, but also effort associated with providing context, prompting, reviewing, correcting, verifying, and integrating AI-generated outputs. Human judgment and accountability remained central, with practitioners anticipating a shift from direct code production to guiding, evaluating, validating, integrating, and coordinating AI-supported work. Thus, GenAI appears to redistribute cognitive work toward oversight rather than simply eliminate it, although whether overall cognitive workload increases or decreases remains undetermined.

authors.name: Chamari Dasanayake, Vladimir Mandi\'c, Rahul Mohanani, Burak Turhan

papers.title: Ask the Peers: Ranking NFR Coverage Gaps for Requirements Review
papers.summary: Missing or underrepresented non-functional requirements (NFR) categories leave little direct evidence in a requirements set, making them difficult to identify during requirements review. In this study, we frame NFR coverage-gap review as a project-level ranking task: given a target requirements specification, the goal is to rank the 11 PROMISE NFR categories for analyst inspection. We compare seven statistical, embedding-based, and large language model (LLM)-based configurations that differ in both ranking mechanism and evidence source, including target requirement statements, peer requirements, their semantic representation, and peer category statistics. We evaluate the configurations using controlled gap injection with leave-one-project-out evaluation on PROMISE, PROMISE+, PURE-Transport, and PURE-Business. Four configurations that use peer category statistics are effectively tied under complete removal (0.875-0.889 mean AUROC), despite different ranking mechanisms, and supplying those statistics to a direct LLM ranker produces the largest evidence gain. All configurations weaken when a category is present but underrepresented, and none is best for every NFR category. For count-changing category-level gaps, structured peer evidence matters more than ranker sophistication. The findings suggest that the rankings should guide analyst inspection rather than serve as automatic judgements of requirements completeness.

authors.name: Risha Parveen, Najmeh Akbari, Farnaz Delirie, Zheying Zhang, Fran\c{c}ois Christophe, Jussi Rasku, Pekka Abrahamsson

papers.title: When Code Works but the License Doesn't: Evaluating License Constraint Handling in Coding Agents
papers.summary: Coding agents increasingly undertake repository-level development, including dependency selection, source modification, and software deployment. However, existing evaluations prioritize functional success over licensing correctness and commercial suitability. We investigate whether agents recognize and preserve software-license constraints when developing proprietary software. Experiments across multiple agents examine permissive and copyleft licenses, missing licensing information, transitive dependencies, source modification, dual licensing, vendoring, and distribution contexts. Agent traces, repository changes, and final artifacts are evaluated against licensing ground truth. Results reveal a persistent gap between functional and licensing correctness. Agents can successfully build and test software while overlooking licensing constraints involving provenance, authorization, and distribution. Better outcomes emerge when licensing information translates into engineering actions such as dependency substitution, architectural changes, and release gating. We argue that licensing in agentic development requires contextual constraint recognition and preservation across the software lifecycle, not merely license classification.

authors.name: Sundaraparipurnan Narayanan, Sandeep Vishwakarma

papers.title: Dependency Fabrication in Repository Deployment Agents
papers.summary: Repository deployment agents set up the environment needed to run a software repository. They often treat passing tests as proof of a successful setup. This report examines how such agents behave when a working setup is impossible. Probe repositories were built with a dependency that the agents could not legitimately obtain. Passing tests therefore indicated fabrication, such as creating a stub to replace the missing package. Agents in Repo2Run and SetupX usually fabricated the dependency. Both harnesses mostly still marked these runs as successful. Rules against fabrication, whether given in the prompt or repository documentation, did not reliably prevent this behavior. On MinimalSetupAgent, which was built for this report, mitigations proposed in the reward-hacking literature were most effective when the agent received a direct rule and had a clear way to stop and report the problem. Under these conditions, neither Qwen3.5-Plus nor GPT-5.6 Luna cheated in any of the 16 runs. Applying the same mitigation to Repo2Run and SetupX also required a native tool call for escalation. In Repo2Run, it worked only after the prompt was also replaced with one that placed less emphasis on passing tests.

authors.name: Robin Matter, Salman Toor

papers.title: Repository-Grounded Rubrics for Execution-Free Evaluation of Coding Agents
papers.summary: Coding agents are usually evaluated by running task-specific tests, but tests may be missing or incomplete, and running them requires a working environment for each repository. We adapt agentic rubrics, introduced for selecting among candidate patches, into an execution-free measure of how far a patch satisfies a task's requirements. An agent explores the repository before the change and writes weighted binary criteria, and a judge without tools scores a diff by the weighted share of criteria it satisfies. We validate the ordering this score produces against test outcomes on SWE-bench Verified, using 7,291 labeled patches from fifteen systems. Within the 400 tasks that have both resolved and unresolved patches, the mean per-task AUROC is 0.826 (0.838 on tasks not used to tune the rubric-generation prompt), and ranking systems by their failing patches closely agrees with ranking them by resolve rate (Spearman 0.968). Case analyses trace disagreements to tests that do not match the task, execution-blocking defects that the textual assessment misses, and errors in criteria or verdicts. The validation does not establish absolute score magnitudes or requirement satisfaction beyond agreement with tests, but rubric scores could complement tests where tests or execution environments cannot be assumed.

authors.name: Matej Gerek, Danylo Zahorulko, Samuel Budai, Chris Rupley, Thierry Donneau-Golencer

papers.title: Reusing formal Vlasov-Maxwell proofs to certify plasma solver outputs
papers.summary: AI now produces machine-checked mathematics faster than researchers can read it. Can such theorems do practical computational work?
