papers.summary: Matter waves can exhibit structured wavefields analogous to those of light, offering new means of controlling the spatial and angular-momentum degrees of freedom of massive particles. Bessel beams are a fundamental class of structured waves that exhibit non-diffracting propagation, self-healing, and well-defined orbital angular momentum (OAM). Here, we experimentally realize neutron Bessel beams by imprinting a nanoscale conical phase gradient onto a neutron wavefront. By incorporating azimuthal phase gradients, we generate zeroth-, third-, and sixth-order Bessel beams, demonstrating direct control of both the OAM and radial structure of a massive particle. We also propose a neutron Bessel-grating interferometer, complementary to established optical and electron interferometric methods, in which varying the radial grating period by approximately 100 nm yields a controlled Gouy phase shift of $\pi$. These results establish neutron Bessel beams as a new platform for diffractive neutron focusing and provide an experimental foundation for theoretical studies of Bessel beams in neutron scattering, decay, and OAM characterization.

authors.name: Owen Lailey, Dusan Sarenac, Nir Emelianenko, Charles W. Clark, David G. Cory, Huseyin Ekinci, Michael G. Huber, Jeremy W. Paster, Anna Sokolova, Diego Alba Venero, Dmitry A. Pushin

papers.title: Modelling population distribution across cities on spatial networks using the kinetic theory of multi-agent systems
papers.summary: We investigate the urban population distribution of the Italian region of Sardinia through the kinetic theory of multi-agent systems on spatial networks, interpreting cities both as agents and vertices of a graph, and representing interurban links as edges. We consider various emigration rules to model the interactions between agents, obtaining two main results: the bimodal lognormal fit of the total population distribution among cities and the Pareto fit of the tail. Overall, our model provides results consistent with the actual distribution derived from ISTAT data of Sardinia; furthermore, the bimodal lognormal fit generally follows the distribution tail more accurately than the Pareto one, although the two coincide in the first half.

authors.name: Valerio Taralli, Andrea Tosin

papers.title: Optical readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors with SiPMs
papers.summary: Scintillation light readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors (MPGDs) is used for imaging and track reconstruction applications including in optical Time Projection Chambers (TPC). Typically, high resolution CCD or CMOS imaging sensors are used and PMTs can be employed to obtain auxiliary timing information. We report on the optical readout of MPGDs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) which enables limited spatial resolution. Arrays of SiPMs were used to read out Gaseous Electron Multipliers (GEMs) and Glass Micromegas amplification stages. Center of gravity reconstruction of hit positions yields a spatial resolution of approximately 1.35 mm for signals shared across multiple SiPMs. High gain of the amplification stage as well as the SiPMs enables good signal sharing and is advantageous for position reconstruction.

authors.name: F. M. Brunbauer, K. J. Fl\"othner, F. Garcia, D. Janssens, E. Jelinkova, M. Lisowska, D. Marques, H. M\"uller, E. Oliveri, E. Pollacco, L. Ropelewski, L. Scharenberg, B. Sch\"onfelder, E. Tuovinen, M. van Stenis, R. Veenhof

papers.title: Physics-based Tabulation Approach for Rotating Detonation Engines
papers.summary: High-fidelity simulations of rotating detonation engines remain computationally expensive due to the strong coupling between compressible flow dynamics and stiff chemical kinetics. The coexistence of deflagrative and detonative combustion, along with shock interactions and rapid thermodynamic changes, further challenges conventional reduced-order chemistry models. This work presents a multi-mode tabulation framework that replaces detailed chemical kinetic integration with precomputed thermochemical states and source terms while accounting for variations in the local thermodynamic state. The key novelty lies in a unified treatment of distinct combustion regimes, wherein homogeneous reactor solutions describe deflagrative combustion and post-detonation reactions up to the Chapman-Jouguet (CJ) point, while an equilibrium isentropic expansion model captures supersonic relaxation beyond the CJ state. The framework is evaluated against detailed chemistry across progressively complex configurations, including homogeneous ignition, one-dimensional detonations, and a two-dimensional rotating detonation engine (RDE). The tabulated model accurately reproduces ignition delays and captures the initiation and sustained propagation of detonation waves across varying mixture compositions. Furthermore, the framework reconstructs the complete thermodynamic evolution along an RDE streamline, including post-injection expansion, detonation, post-detonation expansion, and oblique shock interactions, directly from conserved flow variables. These results demonstrate the capability of multi-mode tabulation to represent coupled combustion, shock, and expansion processes within a single thermodynamically responsive framework, offering a promising route toward computationally efficient simulations of detonative combustion across a broad range of applications.

authors.name: Noah Schwalb, Vansh Sharma, Shivank Sharma, Venkat Raman

papers.title: Scalable Non-Parametric Bayesian Inference of Free Energy Landscapes and Emission Functions from Observations
papers.summary: Free-energy landscapes govern processes from protein conformational change to climate oscillations, but are typically observed only indirectly, through observables such as FRET intensity or optical-tweezer transmittance. Neither the landscape shape, nor the emission function mapping latent state to signal, is usually known, and distinct states may produce the same signal. We therefore infer landscape and emission function jointly and non-parametrically, using the exact non-linear Bayesian filtering likelihood, to fully use the information contained in observable trajectories that are often noisy, scarce and costly to acquire. A novel parallel-in-time algorithm makes this tractable: it is up to 27 times faster than sequential filtering on one GPU, scales near-ideally across GPUs, and, given enough resources, has runtime independent of trajectory length. We demonstrate the method on a single-protein optical tweezer recording, where distinct conformations produce the same signal, and beyond biology on the El Nino-Southern Oscillation and financial market volatility.

authors.name: Eliane Briand, Helmut Grubm\"uller

papers.title: The Structural Number of Parties: An Electoral-Outcome-Independent Baseline for Comparing Party-System Scale
papers.summary: How many parties can a country structurally sustain? Standard measures such as the effective number of parties (ENP) cannot answer this question. They are descriptive and post hoc: they summarize competition only after an election, and they depend on electoral returns that are often missing, interrupted, or unreliable in many developing democracies, particularly in Africa. They also offer no common scale for comparing the size of party registers with realized electoral fragmentation. We introduce the Structural Number of Parties (SNP), an outcome-independent baseline derived from two universally available quantities: population size and territorial area. Building on the logic of the seat product model and the cube-root law of assembly size, the SNP gives an ex ante benchmark that can be computed for any country and year, including where electoral data are absent. Applied to African states, the SNP enables a structural gap diagnosis that distinguishes under-fragmented systems, marked by hegemonic-party dominance, from over-fragmented ones, marked by excessive atomization. The framework thus provides a transparent and reproducible tool to inform institutional reform and the rationalization of party systems across the continent.

authors.name: Adama Nouboukpo, Kodzo Michel Aladji, Bappa Muktar

papers.title: A curvature-corrected port-Hamiltonian reduced-order model for dissipative sloshing with contact-line hysteresis in low-gravity tanks
papers.summary: A physics-based reduced-order model unifies curved-meniscus inertia, viscous losses and nonsmooth contact-line stick-slip in a passive port-Hamiltonian formulation for lateral sloshing in cylindrical tanks. Dirichlet-Neumann and Jacobi operators describe inertia and restoring forces, while a convex potential combines bulk, Stokes-layer and contact-line dissipation. Analytical propagation between stick-slip events supports faster-than-real-time simulation of coupled spacecraft translation and sloshing. The viscous closure agrees within 5% with a reference Stokes calculation, and the model reproduces the Henderson-Miles modal measurements and the Cocciaro hysteretic decay. Across 42 drop-tower and ground measurements, curvature correction reduces the root-mean-square frequency error from 24 to 4%. For flight and ground tests from the Middeck 0-Gravity Dynamics Experiment (MODE), frequency errors range from 0.9 to 7.1%, while ideal contact lines underestimate the damping ratios from the MODE fits by 38-87%. One hysteresis width, calibrated on the lowest orbital water excitation, predicts higher orbital excitations and the ground test with normalised force errors of 11-35%, against 149-208% for an ideal pinned line. It predicts 8.5% resonance softening against 7.3% measured, which the tested one-parameter damping laws miss. Uncertain wetting and remaining response discrepancies motivate damping ranges in spacecraft control analyses.

authors.name: Gianni Cassoni, Fabrizio Gennari, Jacopo Serafini, Pierangelo Masarati

papers.title: GenerativeQC: A Generative, GPU-Accelerated Quantum Chemistry Program
papers.summary: GenerativeQC is an open-source, GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry program that computes energies and analytic nuclear forces from Hartree-Fock (HF) and density functional theory (DFT) to closed-shell density-fitted CCSD(T) and an MP2-assisted CCSD(T)/complete-basis-set (CBS) composite. Its scientific compiler translates symbolic equations into C++ and CUDA code and uses automatic differentiation to generate the derivative and response programs that analytic forces require. A native runtime executes these programs together with hand-written iterative solvers and integral routines. Across HF and DFT benchmarks for eight methods on water clusters of up to 96 atoms, GenerativeQC is faster than GPU4PySCF in all 128 comparisons on an RTX 5090 GPU and in all but two comparisons on an H100 GPU. For correlated wave functions, compiler-generated derivative contractions and transpose Jacobian operators enable complete density-fitted CCSD(T) and CCSD(T)/CBS analytic forces on GPUs, completing a CCSD(T)/CBS energy-and-force calculation for heptane (23 atoms) in 4.5 min on a single H100 GPU (17 min on RTX 5090).

authors.name: Shengrui Xu, Longhan Shen, Wenxi Zhai, Tong Zhu, Jinzhe Zeng

papers.title: Instability of layered two-phase flow in a vertical plane channel
papers.summary: The equilibrium two-phase flows in a vertical plane channel are explored by adopting an approximate Boussinesq-like model. The class of stationary parallel flows examined in this paper features three-layer configurations in which the central core is less dense than the peripheral layers. Such flows are considered purely buoyant, induced by the density difference between the phases. The simplified scheme leads to a formulation where the parameters driving the transition to linear instability of the equilibrium flow are the Archimedes number and the dimensionless positions of the interfaces between the phases. The analysis takes into consideration symmetric and asymmetric flows, including, as special cases, also two-layer configurations with one phase close to the left-hand boundary wall and the other close to the right-hand wall. In particular, the completely antisymmetric flow, where the equilibrium velocity profile is an odd function of the transverse coordinate, shows up as the least stable configuration among those examined in this study.

authors.name: Antonio Barletta, Michele Celli, Vittorio Di Federico, Sandro Longo

papers.title: Polycentrality in Urban Socioecological Systems: A Multilayer Analysis of Social Infrastructure in Iztapalapa, Mexico City
papers.summary: The spatial distribution of infrastructure and activities, along with the networks and interactions that connect them, is key to understanding the relationship between urban form, function, and sustainability from a complex systems perspective. Within this dynamic relationship, the extent to which localized social infrastructure can reinforce existing functional centralities or create conditions for the emergence of new ones remains insufficiently understood. This study examines these relationships through the UTOP\'IAS program in Iztapalapa, Mexico City, where 15 public social facilities have been established across a historically underserved urban territory. We develop a multilayer network framework integrating pedestrian infrastructure, GTFS-based public transport services, and UTOP\'IAS as a target layer to assess multimodal connectivity, travel-time accessibility, and spatial coverage. These conditions are examined alongside indicators of local economic centrality (PCI and wPCI) to investigate how infrastructure interdependencies relate to the functional organization of urban space. The analysis reveals spatial heterogeneity in multimodal accessibility and differences in the integration of UTOP\'IAS with existing transport networks. By relating these patterns to pre-existing economic centralities, we examine whether distributed social infrastructure may reinforce established functional centers or create conditions favorable to emerging centralities, without assuming that spatial decentralization necessarily produces polycentrality. The findings contribute a relational, data-driven approach to understanding how social infrastructure and mobility shape urban functions, emphasizing accessibility and territorial integration as critical conditions for more equitable and sustainable urban development.

authors.name: Marco A. Rosas, Gustavo Carre\'on, Carlos Gershenson, Jes\'us Mario Siqueiros

papers.title: A boundary integral formulation for microscale Marangoni surfing
papers.summary: We consider a model for collections of surfactant-producing particles moving along the surface of a viscous fluid under their self-generated Marangoni flows. Such systems are challenging due to their nonlocal nature: particle motion is coupled to Marangoni stresses distributed across the entire fluid surface and to the resulting flows in the bulk. In the low Reynolds and P\'eclet number limit, we reduce these nonlocal effects to a system of integral equations supported solely on the particles and their boundaries. This formulation is not only computationally tractable, but also provides a framework for systematically coarse-graining many-particle systems. Numerical simulations, performed with a custom spectral method, show collective dynamics are highly sensitive to shape. In particular, among elliptical particles, we find prolate particles tend to attract while oblate particles tend to repel, and these geometric details control the stability of polarized populations. We rationalize these behaviors through a far-field expansion of the boundary integral equations and its corresponding reduced-order model.

authors.name: Scott Weady

papers.title: Design and Modeling of Graded Base III-Nitride HBTs for High-Frequency Applications
papers.summary: This work analyzes the high-frequency performance constraints of AlGaN/GaN heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs) and proposes a novel band-engineered graded base N-polar AlGaN/GaN HBT and evaluates the RF performances. Unlike conventional p-GaN base designs, we propose a graded base in the N-polar orientation which offers polarization-induced hole accumulation with quasi-electric field-assisted minority carrier transport. The proposed design simultaneously mitigates the longstanding current crowding, Webster effect, and conventional base resistance limitations. Using well-calibrated two-dimensional TCAD simulations, the proposed compositionally graded base HBT projects peak f_T/f_{max} of 190/200 GHz with a power density (V_{br}I_{max}/8 > 20 W/mm), offering a promising pathway toward simultaneous high-frequency and high-power GaN millimeter-wave electronics.

authors.name: Md Saklain Morshed, Chandan Joishi, Ijaas Mohamed, Siddharth Rajan

papers.title: xTBloom: GPU Batching for High-Throughput GFN-xTB Calculations
papers.summary: Conformational searches and multiwindow free-energy sampling require large numbers of GFN-xTB energy and force evaluations across molecular conformations and sampling windows. Processing each system separately on a GPU makes it difficult to amortize memory management, host-device data transfer, and kernel-launch overhead. Here, we present xTBloom, a GPU batching library for GFN-xTB energy and force evaluations. xTBloom sorts evaluation queues by atomic orbital (AO) count before forming batches, accommodates size differences through a native ragged layout, maintains independent self-consistent charge (SCC) and failure states for each system, and selects execution paths according to data residency. We focus the quantitative evaluation on GFN2-xTB through cross-program comparisons on QM9 and OMol25, CPU-CUDA comparisons, finite-difference force checks, and controlled failure tests. On a near-size OMol25 workload, GPU execution achieved a 2.9-fold speedup over xTBloom's single-core CPU backend. A companion LAMMPS plugin integrates cross-window batching with periodic quantum mechanical/molecular mechanical (QM/MM) simulation. In a short synchronized test with 48 windows on one GPU, the complete coupled workflow achieved an aggregate speedup of approximately 14 over sequential execution of the same windows. These results demonstrate the throughput benefits of batched GFN-xTB evaluation for repeated electronic-structure calculations and multiwindow sampling.

authors.name: Zitian Lu, Shengrui Xu, Tong Zhu, Qiangqiang Gu, Jinzhe Zeng

papers.title: Consistent interfacial flow numerics - Part I: The gravity force term
papers.summary: The OpenFOAM solver interFoam for incompressible two-phase flows combines the single-phase PISO/PIMPLE algorithm for the pressure-velocity coupling with an interface advection step. It relies on the standard finite volume discretisation of the momentum equation, which assumes smooth fields, but across a water-air interface the density jumps by a factor of about 1000. The geometric Volume-of-Fluid method isoAdvector, used in interIsoFoam, made the advection step consistent with a sharp interface, but spurious velocities near it remain due to the momentum discretisation. This series revisits it term by term. Here we treat the gravity term, which acts only at the interface and depends on the local interface height. Both solvers crudely assign this height using the face centre positions. We show that this is a key source of the spurious air velocities. Taking the height from the reconstructed interface instead gives an exact discrete balance between pressure and gravity for a horizontal interface on any mesh. We implement this geometric gravity model in a new solver, interIsoGoam. In a tilted box of still water, where the original solvers give air speeds of metres per second, it keeps the velocity of order $10^{-9}$ m/s. This holds for density ratios up to $10^7$ and, with a hydrostatic initial pressure, on skewed and locally refined meshes. In a progressive wave, interIsoGoam has the lowest maximum velocity of the three solvers. At maximum Courant numbers of 0.1 and below it therefore needs up to 43 % fewer steps and up to 38 % less wall-clock time. At 0.5 the wave grows by up to 12 % over 15 periods, so we recommend 0.1 or less. One error remains, namely an overprediction of the horizontal water velocity below the wave crest. All three solvers exhibit this error, which grows steadily with time. In Part II we trace this error to the implicit discretisation of the momentum convection term.

authors.name: Johan Roenby, Konstantinos Missios, Kasper M{\o}ller, Sithik Aliyar, Henning Scheufler

papers.title: Raman-induced Kerr effect and heating in diamond
papers.summary: We fully characterize the polarization-dependent third-order nonlinear susceptibility in a diamond crystal using phase-sensitive nondegenerate pump-probe spectroscopy near 1~$\mu$m wavelength. Measuring the frequency-domain phase shift and amplitude change of the probe pulse as a function of polarization and probe wavelength allows direct extraction of the full anisotropic $\chi^{(3)}$ response, including the Raman contribution. We find that the polarization dependence of the two-beam coupling contribution for the Raman component differs from that predicted solely using one-beam selection rules. We measure a Kerr coefficient that is within the range of reported values in the literature, and our measured anisotropy parameters satisfy Kleinman symmetry, as expected. Our measured Raman polarizability agrees, after scaling for its dispersion, with a Brillouin-referenced measurement at 514.5~nm [Grimsditch and Ramdas, Phys. Rev. B \textbf{11}, 3139 (1975)], but is lower than measurements from absolute Raman cross sections. The same technique could be used to measure other materials with relatively high phonon frequencies, and it complements measurements of the Kerr contribution of low-frequency modes using impulsive stimulated Raman scattering (ISRS). When the pump-probe difference frequency matches the phonon resonance, Raman-enabled two-photon absorption occurs; we directly measure the resulting heat deposition in diamond using time-resolved beam deflection of a continuous-wave laser. The measurement technique demonstrated here is capable of precise absolute $\chi^{(3)}$ measurements and will enable quantitative stimulated Raman heating microscopy, with potential extensions to thermal conductivity metrology.

authors.name: C. D. Cruz, J. C. Stephenson, J. K. Wahlstrand

papers.title: Effect of a role model-based show on the STEM aspirations of primary school students
papers.summary: A STEM outreach show called 'Who wants to be a Superhero' went into primary schools across England and Wales, delivered by professional science communicators. The show was structured around four female STEM role models and two male STEM role models as part of a wider narrative about scientists and engineers being real-life superheroes. The show was found to increase both boys' and girls' aspirations for a STEM career, with a bigger effect seen in the girls. The intervention also increased positive attitudes, and decreased negative attitudes, towards scientists measured through word association given by the audiences pre- and post-show. There was a larger reduction in negative stereotypes from the girls after the show, especially in the 'nerdy' and 'crazy' stereotypes. The show saw an increase in both boys' and girls' perceptions of the 'helpful' nature of science and engineering. It was also found that some students may not want to do a STEM job because of the perceived dangerous nature of the job.

authors.name: Wendy Sadler, Sophie Bartlett, Naomi Dinmore

papers.title: Time-Varying Medium from an Ensemble of Laser-Dressed Quantum Emitters
papers.summary: We propose a minimal quantum-mechanical model of a frequency dispersive, time-modulated medium that explicitly incorporates the pumping mechanism. It consists of a homogeneous ensemble of quantum emitters dressed by a pump laser. We analyze their dispersive, time-varying response to a perturbative probe field by deriving the macroscopic polarizability of the ensemble, and then solving Maxwell's equations via the Floquet formalism. This yields a rich band structure that departs from conventional analyses in which the modulation source is neglected, arising from the interplay between the dispersive polaritonic and time-varying responses. These results shed light on the role of the modulation source in time-varying media and pave the way toward realizing dispersive time-varying media from driven quantum-mechanical systems.

authors.name: Adri\'an Juan-Delgado, Diego Mart\'in-Cano, Paloma A. Huidobro

papers.title: Consistent interfacial flow numerics - Part II: The momentum convection term
papers.summary: The two-phase Volume-of-Fluid solvers of OpenFOAM overpredict the horizontal water velocity near the crest of a water wave, and the error grows as the wave propagates. Part I of this series removed the spurious air velocities caused by the gravity term but left this error unchanged. Here we show that it is caused by the momentum convection term. Its mass flux is computed in the interface advection step from the velocity at the start of the time step, whereas the convected velocity is taken at the end of the step, because convection is discretised implicitly. In a progressive wave, where the horizontal and vertical velocities are 90 degrees out of phase, this time lag produces an upward flux of horizontal momentum, proportional to the time step, which accumulates in a spurious current near the surface. The same mismatch makes the response to a force depend on the density at the wrong time level. Explicit convection removes the lag and makes the response consistent with the gravity force, but requires the convected face velocity at the interface to be taken from the upwind cell. Only then is the new velocity of a cell a weighted average of old velocities, whatever the density ratio. We demonstrate both requirements with prescribed flows and with the full solver. For a progressive wave, explicit convection with upwind face velocities at the interface reduces the overprediction of the crest velocity from 26-31 % to within 1 % and removes the near-surface current. The resulting solver, fluxinator, is meant for maximum Courant numbers of 0.1 and below, where it keeps the wave height within 1.5 % over 15 periods on meshes with six or more cells per wave height. Because the spurious velocities that limit the time step are removed, it needs 34-42 % less wall-clock time than interFoam for the tested wave.

authors.name: Johan Roenby

papers.title: Kinetic study of Reaction-Control-Jet Interference in Rarefied Hypersonic Crossflow
papers.summary: A 1975 wind-tunnel study at the German Aerospace Center (DLR) of a helium jet blowing from a flat plate into a Mach 11 to 12 air crossflow at three freestream densities is revisited using two- and three-dimensional Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) computations at Knudsen numbers 0.021 to 0.125. The planar slot used in two-dimensional model computations reproduces the shock topology, the sign and two-lobed structure of the interference pressure and its trend with rarefaction, and its plate-alone boundary layer is consistent with the three-dimensional one and with a similarity solution with slip and temperature jump. However, two-dimensional simulations overpredict the peak interference pressure about twelvefold at every condition and carry it farther upstream. A resolution sweep at the most rarefied condition converges the planar interference to within 1% of its extrapolated limit. Three-dimensional DSMC reproduces the measured interference pressure at all three densities, within 25% at the lobe peak and 3 mm in its position, although two- and three-dimensional simulations overpredict the plate-alone wall pressure by 50 to 75%. Continuum breakdown around the jet persists even at the lowest Knudsen number examined. Fully three-dimensional kinetic simulations are underway to extend the present validation to a comparison of jet strength and forces over wider Knudsen number ranges, and to an examination of lateral relief as a reason for the discrepancy.

authors.name: Alexis Theofilis, Martin Grabe

papers.title: Toward high-throughput, low-latency structural biology using light, Part I: Protein-ligand pose determination
papers.summary: We demonstrate for the first time that an optical spectroscopy - electron-vibration-vibration two-dimensional infrared spectroscopy (EVV 2DIR) - has sufficient structural competence to enable the reconstruction of the three-dimensional geometries of drug-protein binding at the level needed for practical drug discovery applications. Klug et al. previously demonstrated experimental detection of drug binding to a kinase using EVV 2DIR. Here we use a quantum mechanical approach to calculate and assign elements of EVV 2DIR spectra for the spectral region 1200-1800 cm$^{-1}$ / 1100-1800 cm$^{-1}$ of 92 protein-ligand complexes. This dataset includes ligand-target poses drawn from existing crystal structures and ligand-target poses created by docking and cofolding models. We find that binding-dependent spectral features are robust, interpretable, and consistent across poses in a given binding mode, and distinct for each unique hydrogen bonding geometry. We construct a spectral distance metric to distinguish poses that conform to the ligand-target hydrogen-bonding pattern of the crystal structure from those that do not. These results show that, given a set of predicted ligand-target poses containing the correct geometry, the hydrogen-bonding pattern of the valid pose may be rapidly identified by comparing simulated and experimental EVV 2DIR spectra. Finally, we discuss the practical implications for a new, high throughput structural biology for drug discovery that will be the subject of forthcoming manuscripts, noting that the base technologies to perform EVV 2DIR quickly and efficiently already exist and will enable a novel structure to be determined in only minutes for each sample. Moreover, this can be achieved without the need for crystallization, isotopic labeling, or low temperatures, non-destructively using picogram quantities of material.

authors.name: Brian K. Petkov, David R. Klug

papers.title: The role of externally-driven density fluctuations in the enhancement of beam spray
papers.summary: Speckled laser beams, commonly used to ionize and heat plasma for inertial confinement fusion and high-energy-density experiments, are shown to drive long-wavelength plasma-density fluctuations that induce beam spray in other laser beams. Experiments show that a 1053 nm beam undergoes increased beam spray when 351 nm speckled heater beams are on. These observations indicate that the high-intensity speckles sustain an increased level of steady-state density fluctuations. Modeling of these fluctuations predicts amplitudes that are orders of magnitude larger than the level of thermal fluctuations. Beam propagation simulations show increased beam spray due to self-focusing and filamentation when heater-driven density fluctuations are included.

authors.name: Kyle R. McMillen, Ian D. Min-Roberts, Russell K. Follett, Avram L. Milder, Joseph Katz, Daniel J. Haberberger, Julieta Hernandez Gordillo, Pierre A. Michel, Hans G. Rinderknecht, David Turnbull, John P. Palastro, Dustin H. Froula, Wojciech Rozmus, Jessica L. Shaw

papers.title: Strong Epsilon-Near-Zero Confinement and Interface-Controlled Dynamics in Inverse-Designed Transparent Conducting Oxide Cavities
papers.summary: Achieving optical modulation that is both strong and ultrafast remains a central challenge in time-varying photonics. Here, we theoretically demonstrate that combining inverse-designed cavities that utilize transparent conducting oxides (TCOs) operating at the epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) point with boundaries that support carrier transport can meet this requirement. This is achieved by leveraging ENZ-enhanced optical absorption and electron heating with interface-engineered carrier relaxation. A multilayer inverse-design framework, combined with a structural disorder-aware correction loop, is developed to preserve robust resonant absorption in ultrathin TCO films under realistic material disorder. Relative to conventional TCO cavity geometries, the inverse-designed structures exhibit stronger light confinement, greater electron temperature modulation, and markedly faster recovery. Beyond cavity design, interfacial barrier engineering and adjacent-layer doping emerge as effective degrees of freedom for co-designing spectral and temporal dynamics. Furthermore, our theoretical framework shows that the inverse-designed cavity supports richer oscillatory transmittance dynamics on the few-optical-cycle timescale compared to its single-film counterpart, with interfacial control enabling further temporal compression. The combined control of optical confinement and interfacial dynamics establishes inverse-designed TCO cavities as a viable platform for time-varying photonic media capable of supporting strong and ultrafast optical responses.

authors.name: Jae Ik Choi, Ludmila J. Prokopeva, Vahagn Mkhitaryan, Yuheng Chen, Alexander V. Kildishev, Vladimir M. Shalaev, Alexandra Boltasseva

papers.title: Residual Allan Stability under Periodic Auxiliary Ramsey Sampling
papers.summary: The timing of auxiliary Ramsey measurements can change the frequency stability associated with a drifting pulse shift at a fixed nominal Fisher-information rate for a constant shift. For periodic instantaneous observations of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck shift with causal prediction between updates, we derive the exact residual covariance averaged over the update cycle and the corresponding Allan variance at arbitrary averaging times. Relative to a continuous Kalman reference at the same information rate, periodic estimation increases the cycle-averaged estimation-error variance, reduces the short-time residual Allan variance, and increases its long-time value. Its covariance decays more slowly at the origin and has a larger integral. We extend the result to instantaneous sensing of the sum of finitely many independent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck modes. Integrated observations preserve the short-time ordering for the scalar shift, and numerical calculations resolve the dependence of the crossover on window duration. A zero-order-hold comparison shows that the short-time ordering can change when the same estimator drives a different correction command. A three-level Ramsey model of coherent population trapping (CPT) maps the discriminator response to an effective information budget and illustrates how the dark times affect the choice of schedule.

authors.name: Zhiqian Su

papers.title: Quantum-classical dynamical density functional theory for solvation dynamics
papers.summary: We provide a unified modeling framework for thermalization and non-equilibrium spectroscopy in overdamped polar environments. This framework extends dynamical density functional theory to describe the coupled quantum-classical evolution of a molecular electronic subsystem and an overdamped polar solvent represented by a reaction-field coordinate. The nonadiabatic dynamics is formulated in terms of an operator-valued distribution obeying a quantum-classical Ehrenfest--Smoluchowski equation which exhibits nonlinear classical diffusion and non-increasing free energy, thereby retaining detailed balance. In contrast, a quantum-classical Liouville--Smoluchowski model with quantum-classical linear diffusion develops unstable long-time behavior and fails to reach a stationary thermal state. The method is applied to a two-level model of a polar dye in three different solvents: chloroform, dichloromethane, and dimethyl sulfoxide, each differing in polarity and dielectric relaxation time. Absorption and time-resolved emission spectra are obtained from dipole-dipole correlation functions, capturing the solvent-induced spectral broadening, the dynamic Stokes shift, and the time evolution of the emission bandwidth. The calculated solvent spectral response agrees well with the experimental relaxation trends of the three solvents.

authors.name: Paul Bergold, Irene Burghardt, Francesco Di Maiolo, Cesare Tronci

papers.title: Color Through Time: Distributions, Sparsity and Dominance in Western Painting
papers.summary: We investigate the evolution of color in Western painting using a large corpus of digitized artworks. Each painting is represented by its distribution over a fixed palette of colors in a perceptually uniform space. We compare the color distributions of historical periods and artistic movements through their Jensen-Shannon distances, and introduce two interpretable descriptors, sparsity and dominance, that quantify how many colors are used and how unevenly they are represented. We find a historical transition from dark, earthy palettes toward a broader and more saturated chromatic range, unfolding through distinct shifts from the nineteenth century onward. Periods evolve smoothly over time, whereas artistic movements display increasingly distinct chromatic signatures beyond chronology. In the sparsity-dominance plane, painting follows a two-stage historical trajectory, first broadening the range of colors used and later increasing color dominance. Comparison with natural images reveals distinct ways in which artistic palettes depart from nature, either through the colors they use or through how broadly and evenly those colors are distributed. Finally, two surveys on generated images show that judgments of harmonious color balance concentrate around two complementary regimes: many colors arranged in a strong hierarchy, or few colors used evenly.

authors.name: Ortensia Forni, Alexandre Darmon, Michael Benzaquen

papers.title: Does a label survive the loop? A screen of necessary physical conditions for a self-measuring system, with a pre-registered test on fly connectomes
papers.summary: Theories that tie experience to a system that re-reads its own state rarely say what a physical substrate must supply for such a loop to run. We state necessary conditions as measurable bounds in one currency: the number of rounds, each one write, hold and re-read, that a written label survives.A floor follows from fundamental constants. Tier 1 asks whether a carrier can hold the label; it is the published quality-factor screen, restated in rounds and extended to a population code. Tier 2 bounds how many rounds a quantum resource survives in a loop that keeps a record. Tier 3 asks whether a network contains a compartment, a set of neurons that a random walk leaves more slowly than it mixes inside. Tier 4 compares what the loop and an outside observer can recover. We implement Tiers 3 and 4 on three connectomes of Drosophila. Exploration of two animals singled out the heading system of the ellipsoid body. Five criteria were then registered and run once on a third animal, and all were met with all connections counted. One was met narrowly, and two fail in that data set when connections of one or two synapses are removed, which we trace in part to synapse detection. As a population code the heading label holds about two bits for seven seconds. The screen can exclude substrates. Passing it is not evidence of experience.

authors.name: Eran Kopel

papers.title: Why supersonic UAP events are not accompanied by acoustic booms?
papers.summary: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) events have been recorded for decades. However, the nature of these events remains unknown. We advocate an idea that the dark matter (DM) in form of the axion quark nuggets (AQN) made of standard model quarks (or {\it antiquarks}) and gluons could {\it simultaneously} explain many observed puzzling features which always accompany the UAP events, such as high velocity, enormous acceleration, absence of any remaining materials in affected area, etc. This long list of mysterious features also includes the absence of any sound which normally accompanies any supersonic motion. The AQN framework answers this last puzzle as well, which represents the title of the present work. The AQN dark matter model was invented long ago without any intension to apply the model to UAP events. Rather, it was invented with a single motivation to explain the observed similarity $\Omega_{\rm DM}\sim \Omega_{\rm visible}$ between visible and DM components, which represents a very generic feature of this framework, not sensitive to any parameters of the construction. In this work we use the same framework with the same set of parameters to study the observed UAP events. Essentially we argue that a specific class of UAP represents the close cousin of other mysteries known for decades (even centuries), such as sky-quakes, Ball Lightnings, and Mysterious Transient events. In other words, the UAPs represent different manifestations of exactly the same objects, the AQNs propagating in atmosphere. The fuel powering all these mysterious energetic events is one and the same: it is the antiquark core of the AQNs. We also present some suggestions on type of instruments required to study this specific (and well defined) type of the UAP events.

authors.name: Ariel Zhitnitsky

papers.title: The Price of Discovery: Cost-Optimized Detectors for the GUT-Scale QCD Axion
papers.summary: Grand unification and string theory point to a quantum chromodynamics (QCD) axion with mass between $10^{-11}$ and $10^{-8}$ eV, while heterotic string theory suggests a mass of $0.5-0.8$ neV. We study which laboratory experiment could discover or exclude DFSZ-strength QCD axion dark matter at and above 0.5 neV at the lowest cost, which we estimate from scaling laws calibrated to historical data. We find that a lumped-element detector, building on the ABRACADABRA concept, can do so with demonstrated readout technology; an example is a shielded toroid about 14 m across with a 6 T NbTi magnet, whose magnet and cryostat we estimate at around 120 million Swiss francs (MCHF). If projected readout targets are met, a 5 m toroid at 25 MCHF suffices. We find these designs by optimizing the toroid, solenoid, and core lumped-element topologies under a common cost metric. The toroid emerges as the most promising and cost-effective topology. The optimal field of the toroid detector is far below the 16 T of the proposed DMRadio-GUT design, which would cost nearly twice as much as our optimum. Heterodyne searches with superconducting radio-frequency cavities, with cavity shapes that we optimize for price, cost between about the same as and twice as much as the lumped-element detectors, but require cavities of volumes $\sim50-2000$ m$^3$. We find that nuclear-magnetic-resonance searches (CASPEr) need orders-of-magnitude gains in spin polarization and coherence. We release axionMultiPhysics, an open-source finite-element and multiphysics package for, e.g., magnetoquasistatic and full-wave electromagnetics, superconductors, readout circuits, and mechanics, from which most of our numerical results were obtained.

authors.name: Joshua N. Benabou, Joshua W. Foster, Benjamin R. Safdi

papers.title: Collective Superconducting-Qubit Interfaces for Microwave-to-Optical Quantum Transduction
papers.summary: Microwave-to-optical quantum transduction is essential for connecting superconducting quantum processors through optical networks. Mechanically mediated transducers, however, remain limited by weak electromechanical coupling, dissipation, and added noise. In this work, we study a transducer in which an ensemble of superconducting qubits couples collectively to a shared optomechanical resonator. For weak signals, we show that ensemble size and optical pump strength together set the conversion efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth, with pump heating limiting efficiency to a finite optimal pump strength. Near half excitation, the collective coupling grows nearly linearly with ensemble size, accelerating transfer of an excitation into the mechanics. We show that this speedup is offset by relaxation of the additional excited qubits, so the single-qubit coupling and lifetime still set the coherence requirement. Transferring exactly one excitation also requires an anharmonic mechanical mode, which an auxiliary qubit coupled to the mechanics can provide. In a lossless prescribed-Kerr benchmark with four qubits and $g_{\rm sm}/(2\pi)=3.81\,\mathrm{kHz}$, a mechanical anharmonicity of $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ raises the final joint single-photon intracavity target probability from $19.6\%$ to $99.7\%$. Finally, we quantify the effects of decoherence, disorder, residual qubit--qubit interactions, and pump-induced qubit noise, finding that pair-dependent interactions reduce the optical retrieval efficiency from 58\% to 35\%. These results establish the coherence and selectivity requirements for collective quantum transduction.

authors.name: Nicolas Dirnegger, Matthew Guibord, William Munizzi, Chee Wei Wong, Prineha Narang

papers.title: Symmetry classification of hyperfine rovibrational molecular phase space
papers.summary: Symmetry-based structures have advanced molecular spectroscopy and quantum information science, yet connections between these fields remain largely unexplored. We construct a phase space theory of a molecule by jointly treating rotational, vibrational, and nuclear-spin degrees of freedom as the quotient of orientations and normal coordinates by the molecule's point group. The various combinations of how these three degrees of freedom transform under symmetries organize a molecule's states into molecular species, and we show that each species is defined by a particular absolutely maximally entangled (AME) carrier state, or, for 45 species, by a two-dimensional space of them. Up to local unitaries and the order of the sectors, molecular species realize 21 AME states across 75 point groups: a product state, four maximally entangled pairs, and 16 genuinely tripartite states. A Fourier transform on the quotient relates orientation and angular-momentum descriptions while preserving these carrier states. We propose an example experimental protocol for preparing and driving symmetry-adapted bend states of $\mathrm{CaOCH_3}$.

authors.name: Elin Ranjan Das, Jing-Chen Zhang, Victor V. Albert, Yuan Liu

papers.title: How the material world of the brain, as a complex system governed by intermittent dynamics, gives rise to the supposedly "immaterial" world of mental processes such as thought
papers.summary: In this paper, we argue that the brain is a complex dynamical system in a critical state similar to that of the 3D Ising model. We highlight several properties of the brain, including resonance phenomena within this critical state, long-range autocorrelations consistent with long memory, a hysteresis zone suggesting the presence of an as yet undetected "exotic" type of matter within the brain, and possible quantum phenomena within the microtubules of neural networks. The latter suggests that these structures exhibit a combined form of "logical superposition". In the proposed model, "AND" logic would require two distinct quantum states to be occupied simultaneously. The proposed "OR" logic allows any one of several quantum states to be occupied at a time. Moreover, we propose that kink and antikink solitons could mediate coupling between occupied quantum states in the microtubules and thereby contribute to pattern formation in neural networks. This mechanism may well be what gives the brain the flexibility to support complex thought and other cognitive functions.

authors.name: Yiannis F. Contoyiannis, Alexandros K. Karlis

papers.title: Quantitative Modeling of Action-Potential-Driven Sodium Dynamics in Neurons: From Sodium Influx to Sodium MRI
papers.summary: Neuronal action potentials are accompanied by the influx of extracellular sodium ions (Na+) into axons through voltage-gated sodium channels. Repetitive neuronal firing can lead to activity-dependent increases in intracellular sodium concentration, which are subsequently reversed primarily through the Na+/K+-ATPase. Quantifying these dynamic changes provides a biophysical foundation for investigating neuronal activity using sodium (23Na) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This mini-review examines the relationships among firing frequency, action-potential-driven sodium influx, and intracellular sodium accumulation, to establish a quantitative framework linking neuronal activity to sodium MRI. The potential sensitivity and limitation of conventional and compartment-sensitive sodium MRI for detecting activity-dependent sodium changes are also discussed. Keywords: Sodium MRI; neuronal firing; action potential; sodium influx; intracellular sodium concentration.

authors.name: Yongxian Qian

papers.title: Deep-Learning-Assisted Full Waveform Inversion for Attenuation Reconstruction in Ultrasound Computed Tomography
papers.summary: Acoustic attenuation is more challenging to reconstruct and has received less attention than sound speed in ultrasound computed tomography using full-waveform inversion (FWI). In this study, a deep-learning (DL)-assisted FWI framework was proposed for attenuation reconstruction based on our previous work. Some numerical experiments were conducted to investigate the strategy and the effectiveness of using DL to help accelerate and improve the reconstruction quality of attenuation imaging in FWI. The results indicated that DL saved computational cost by 28% and improved attenuation reconstruction accuracy by 70% when combined with sufficiently accurate sound speed estimates. The result supports the potential of DL initialization to improve the computational efficiency and reconstruction quality of joint SOS and attenuation FWI.

authors.name: Mingrui Liu, Michael L. Oelze

papers.title: Relative periodic orbits of a free spinning loop
papers.summary: A closed elastic string with no external forces can hold any shape while its material moves steadily along the curve (a steady axial motion), because its tension and the force needed to turn the material around a bend are both proportional to the curvature. I compute the periodic motions that grow from the simplest of these motions, the spinning ring, by Newton's method on a chain of masses. They include rotating waves that turn at twice the rotation rate of the material, standing "flappers" with two to five lobes, and period-doubled and period-tripled orbits. The chain only approximates the string. The orbits and their strong instabilities change little with more masses and are properties of the continuous string. Most weak instabilities change with the number of masses and are artifacts of approximating the string by a finite chain. The saddle flapper of a loop stretched 30% beyond its natural length is neutrally stable at small heights and unstable at large ones. An unstable saddle flapper trades energy back and forth with an in-plane oval, and at large amplitude the energy spreads to the shortest waves of the chain. For Keller's linear string, whose tension is proportional to the stretched length, every motion is periodic, and every knot carries an exactly periodic flapper. For a Hookean string the curvature of a knot couples a ripple to stretching waves that travel at a different speed, and in the simulations a ripple on a sliding knot does not return to its starting shape. Whether a Hookean knot carries any periodic flapper is open.

authors.name: Nicholas B. Tufillaro

papers.title: MAIC-2 v2.3: A Fortran program for simulating the surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation of the planet Mars
papers.summary: The Mars Atmosphere-Ice Coupler MAIC-2 is a computationally efficient, zonally-averaged model designed to simulate Martian surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation over timescales of 10^5 to 10^7 years. While sophisticated General Circulation Models (GCMs) provide high-resolution simulations of the Martian atmosphere, their high computational cost makes them largely unsuitable for studies covering millions of years of orbital evolution. MAIC-2 addresses this gap by utilizing physically-based, zonally-averaged parameterizations, including a Local Insolation Temperature (LIT) scheme and a mass balance engine driven by free-convection and instantaneous mixing physics. Version 2.3 introduces a fully modularized Fortran architecture that improves maintainability and ensures that the software remains entirely self-contained, requiring no external numerical libraries or specialized data formats for execution. Demonstrated through a 20-million-year transient simulation, the model successfully reproduces the primary characteristics of the Martian polar layered deposits. MAIC-2 provides the planetary science community with a versatile, open-source tool for investigating the long-term climatic impacts of orbital variations on the Martian surface.

authors.name: Ralf Greve, Bj\"orn Grieger, Oliver J. Stenzel

papers.title: Kernel Design in Particle Mesh Ewald Methods: Splitting, Interpolation, and Upsampling
papers.summary: For more than thirty years, particle mesh Ewald (PME) methods have dominated the computation of electrostatic interactions in molecular dynamics. A PME method uses a splitting kernel to divide the interaction into a local part, summed within a cutoff, and a smooth part, computed on a grid with a spreading and interpolation (SI) kernel. The established methods use Ewald's Gaussian split with B-spline SI kernels, and the recent Ewald summation with prolates accelerates them severalfold by using a prolate spheroidal wave function (PSWF) for both kernels. Neither choice meets two needs of molecular dynamics: a smooth energy, which long simulations need in order to conserve it, and a low-order SI kernel that stays accurate on coarse grids and gains accuracy as the grid is refined. We present a framework for designing both kernels to meet these needs. For inverse powers from the Coulomb to the dispersion interaction, our splits make the local part smooth at the cutoff to any order while keeping the Fourier concentration of the smooth part close to optimal. We show that with analytic differentiation, the force error of a continuous SI kernel of fixed shape vanishes under grid refinement only if every particle, wherever it lies, gives the grid its exact charge and dipole moment. Our SI kernel for the Coulomb interaction ensures this by construction and is twice continuously differentiable. Compared with the B-spline of the same order, it needs fewer grid points by a factor of up to nearly five; on coarse grids, it mostly needs a lower order than the PSWF kernel. In simulations of liquid water over 100 million time steps, the new kernels reduce the energy drift of both the established and the PSWF kernels by about three orders of magnitude, with a smaller force error than either. Existing PME codes can adopt them by replacing only the two kernels and the Fourier multiplier.

authors.name: Shidong Jiang, Jiuyang Liang, Libin Lu

papers.title: Technical Note on Matlantis PFP v9: Extending the Element and Domain Coverage of the r2SCAN Training Data
papers.summary: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) make atomistic simulations possible at scales beyond the reach of density functional theory (DFT). Matlantis PFP is a uMLIP that treats a variety of domains, including crystals, molecules, and surfaces, with a single model. PFP v8 incorporated a training dataset computed with the r2SCAN functional, chosen for its good agreement with experiment, but the elements and domains covered by that dataset were limited. Here we present Matlantis PFP v9, in which the training data computed with the r2SCAN functional are extended to the lanthanides from Pr to Lu and to the elements from Po to Cm, for a total of 96 elements, and to additional domains such as clusters and adsorption structures. The formation energies of crystals containing the newly supported elements reproduce experimental standard enthalpies of formation with the same level of accuracy as crystals composed only of previously supported elements, and the adsorption energies of molecules on transition-metal surfaces have an overall error against experiment comparable to that of DFT-PBE, although chemisorbed species are overbound. On the same type of GPU (A100), the inference speed and the maximum system size exceed those of SevenNet-Omni, a public uMLIP trained on r2SCAN data: forces are evaluated three to four times faster, and five to ten times as many atoms can be handled. As a result, PFP-R2SCAN is now applicable to systems containing rare-earth and actinide elements and to adsorption on surfaces.

authors.name: Daiki Shintani, Shigeru Iwase, Jun Oshiki, Kohei Shinohara, Nontawat Charoenphakdee, Makoto Hiramatsu, Yuta Tsuboi, Yusuke Asano, Hirotaka Akita, Yong-Bin Zhuang, So Takamoto, Chikashi Shinagawa

papers.title: Projected Sensitivity of a Differential Torsion Sensor for Tests of the Weak Equivalence Principle
papers.summary: Tests of the weak equivalence principle (WEP) are among the most sensitive probes of new long-range, composition-dependent interactions beyond general relativity and the Standard Model. We evaluate the potential of a differential torsion sensor, which combines long mechanical coherence times with optical-cavity readout and common-mode rejection, for laboratory WEP tests and fifth-force searches. For a representative configuration based on an existing prototype, with Be-Ti test masses and 180 days of coherent integration, the projected noise-limited sensitivity to the E\"otv\"os parameter is $\eta\simeq7.5\times10^{-16}$ and $2.4\times10^{-16}$ for signal modulation at 2 and 20 mHz, respectively, below current ground-based torsion-balance limits. For a baryon-coupled Yukawa interaction sourced by the Earth, the corresponding projected sensitivity to the coupling strength is $\alpha\simeq3.1\times10^{-13}$ and $9.8\times10^{-14}$ for ranges $\lambda\gtrsim10^{7}$ m. We identify the modulation scheme, the material contrast, and the source geometry as the main factors that set the projected reach, and the control of systematic couplings as the main experimental requirement for attaining it. These results indicate that differential torsion sensors are a promising platform for future laboratory WEP tests.

authors.name: Jiayi Qin, Sheon S. Y. Chua, Ling Sun, Bram J. J. Slagmolen

papers.title: General Noise Channels and Mid-Circuit Measurements for Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batched Execution
papers.summary: Many studies of quantum protocols require fast sampling of large amounts of measurement data from noisy quantum circuits, such as for training machine-learning decoders for quantum error correction. Exact simulation of realistic noise is expensive, while stabilizer-based simulators are fast but approximate, for example through Pauli twirling, which generally alters the output statistics. Pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) accelerates exact trajectory simulation by sampling noise before state evolution. This method requires the outcome probability of every stochastic event to be independent of the state, which excludes mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels. We present a generalization of PTSBE to measurement and Kraus operators without approximation. Each event is partially pre-sampled, while deferred outcomes are drawn during grouped execution via multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. We implement the method for GPUs as an extension of CUDA-Q. On distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, it is up to 24x faster than conventional trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q. On 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, it is up to 83x faster and outperforms the near-Clifford simulator Clifft when more than about 25% of the gates are non-Clifford. With repeated sampling of each final state, its sampling rate per trajectory exceeds that of CUDA-Q by nearly five orders of magnitude. Our method also allows us to compare exact amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled channel on a surface-code memory, revealing that twirling overestimates the detection rate by 21% and raises the logical error rate of a lookup decoder by 8%. This work makes exact, high-throughput simulation practical for general noisy circuits, from data generation for training decoders to studying measurement-based fault-tolerant protocols under realistic noise.

authors.name: Louis Follet, Paavai Pari, Isidor Schoch, Thien Nguyen, Justin G. Lietz, Daniel Lowell, Brucek Khailany, Krysta M. Svore, Dirk R. Englund, Taylor L. Patti

papers.title: Quantum Mpemba effect in a driven-dissipative atom-waveguide coupled system
papers.summary: The quantum Mpemba effect (QME) describes the counterintuitive phenomenon in which a more strongly perturbed quantum system relaxes toward its steady state faster than a less perturbed one. Here, we investigate the QME in a weakly driven-dissipative atomic array coupled to a one-dimensional chiral waveguide. Starting from the steady state, we introduce a local quench by resetting a single atom to its ground state and examine the subsequent relaxation dynamics. We find that quenching atoms near the array boundaries induces faster initial relaxation through enhanced coupling to superradiant modes and direct photon emission into the waveguide, giving rise to an edge-enhanced QME. Strong directional decay further amplifies this effect by promoting the spatial accumulation of superradiant modes near the preferred boundary, leading to a skin-enhanced QME. At later times, relaxation is increasingly governed by long-lived subradiant modes localized predominantly in the bulk of the array. By coupling two atomic arrays with different interparticle spacings, we further demonstrate an interface-induced QME, where quenching an atom near the interface makes the system relax more slowly at early times but approach its steady state faster at later times, owing to weak participation in both superradiant and subradiant modes. Our findings reveal how the spatial structure of collective decay modes and directional dissipation jointly govern anomalous quantum relaxation, offering potential routes toward accelerated steady-state preparation in waveguide QED systems.

authors.name: Hao-Kai Chi, H. H. Jen

papers.title: Observation of room-temperature intrinsic antiferroelectricity in van der Waals NbOCl2
papers.summary: In recent years, two-dimensional (2D) ferroelectricity has been extensively investigated across a wide range of 2D materials, while intrinsic 2D antiferroelectricity remains exceptionally rare, limiting its implementation in next-generation photonic and electronic devices. Here, we report the observation of room-temperature-stable antiferroelectricity in the layered transition metal oxyhalide NbOCl2, and demonstrate a reversible, stimuli-driven antiferroelectric-to-ferroelectric (AFE-to-FE) phase transition in this material. Second-harmonic generation (SHG) mapping reveals a well-defined stripe-like spatial distribution of SHG intensity across as-grown NbOCl2 flakes spanning thickness from few-layer to bulk-like configurations. This distinctive SHG signature originates from the existence of antiferroelectric phase and the coexistence of antiferroelectric and ferroelectric phases within individual crystals, as evidenced by a combined incident-angle-dependent SHG measurement and Raman spectroscopy. By integrating NbOCl2 with one-dimensional silver nanowires, we achieve spatially selective, strain-mediated AFE-to-FE phase transition. Moreover, an ultralow electric field (~20 kV/cm) induces a reversible SHG response, consistent with switching from the centrosymmetric antiferroelectric state (SHG-silent) to the non-centrosymmetric ferroelectric state (SHG-active). This study not only expands the family of room-temperature 2D antiferroelectrics but also establishes a versatile platform for dynamic manipulation of nonlinear light, paving the way toward electric-field-programmable nonlinear photonics and optical information processing.

authors.name: JinKai Huo, Xingyu Chen, Gaolei Zhao, Xuan Chen, Yuchen Meng, Xu Han, Juhe Liu, Egor Kolesov, Konstantin Kozadaev, Alexei Tolstik, Andrei Zheltkovich, Andrey Novitsky, Shenghuang Lin, Changsen Sun, Dawei Li

papers.title: Rabi-Engineered spin-selective transport of bright soliton in a binary spin-1/2 condensate
papers.summary: Spintronics is usually concentrated on spin-dependent dynamics of single particles such as electrons or holes in solids. Extending this concept to nonlinear matter waves offers an interesting possibility of controlling the transport of collective, particle-like excitations through their spin degrees of freedom. Recent advances in Bose-Einstein condensates have provided a versatile platform for realizing nonlinear spin-1/2 systems that support particle-like objects such as bright solitons, making studies of the motion of these solitons under external fields an interesting and important problem. Here, we study the dynamics of bright solitons with different spin symmetries moving in a coordinate-dependent Rabi field, which acts analogously to a spatially varying magnetic field. In that setup, the velocity perturbed soliton motion possesses very interesting scattering dynamics for both perfect and lifted Manakov symmetry. Lastly, we compare both the velocity-controlled scattering problem with the well-known Rabi quenching protocol. This comparison provides a powerful approach to control the soliton dynamics that may open an avenue to control nonlinear spintronics with solitons as spin carriers.

authors.name: Swarup K. Sarkar, Sh. Mardonov, E. Ya. Sherman, Pankaj K. Mishra

papers.title: Machine learning interatomic potentials and orientational defects in polymers
papers.summary: Photopolymerization of acrylated epoxidized soybean oil (AESO) is a convenient model of a self-organizing process in a soft, bio-based material: ultraviolet light starts a free-radical chain reaction, the growing network releases heat, and the mobility of molecular groups changes on several time scales at once. We follow this process from two sides. Experimentally, the real and imaginary parts of the dielectric permittivity of an AESO:VDM (1:0.5) mixture with 3 mol% of the photoinitiator DMPA were recorded at 500-5000 Hz under an intermittent on/off illumination protocol, and the resulting time series were analysed with a sliding-window Shannon entropy and the Grassberger-Procaccia correlation integral. Both measures show that short light pulses at the start of curing trigger strongly correlated, collective relaxation, which fades as the network forms, leaving only localized reorientations active. We describe these reorientations as orientational defects and quantify their energetics with the MACE-OFF23 machine learning interatomic potential, using relaxed dihedral scans of five rotational modes ($\alpha$, $\alpha/\beta$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$) of an AESO fragment. Compared with density functional theory (DFT) reference profiles, MACE reproduces the shape of all five profiles (Pearson $r=0.95$-$0.98$) and the hierarchy of barriers - from 2.9 eV for the constrained main-chain rotation, through 0.54-0.81 eV for the acrylate rotations, to 0.16-0.18 eV for the methyl and 0.06 eV for the hydroxyl rotation - while underestimating the barrier heights by 3-20%. A simple Arrhenius estimate shows that the acrylate rotations are the modes closest to the frequency window of the dielectric measurement.

authors.name: Arnold Kiv, Volodymyr Soloviev, Andrii Tuzhykov, Andrii Bielinskyi, Taras Kavetskyy, Nataliia Hoivanovych, Ondrej \v{S}au\v{s}a, Jaroslav Rusn\'ak, Helena \v{S}vajdlenkov\'a, Jolita Ostrauskaite, Mykola Slusarenko

papers.title: A probabilistic analysis of the Brumadinho tailings dam-breach using uncertainty quantification and global sensitivity analysis
papers.summary: On 25th January 2019, Dam B1 in Brumadinho, Brazil, suddenly collapsed and produced a catastrophic tailings flow with severe human, environmental and infrastructural consequences. Previous numerical back-analyses of the tailings flow have relied on deterministic approaches, which provide useful reference results but do not explicitly incorporate uncertainty associated to rupture hydrograph and tailings' physical properties. This work presents a probabilistic approach to study the tailings dam-breach flow caused by the rupture of Dam B1, focusing on the quantification and interpretation of the effects of input uncertainty on hazard-related hydrodynamical outputs. Deterministic data was obtained through HEC-RAS v6.6 by considering tailings as an one-phase Bingham fluid. The probabilistic framework combines dimensionality reduction, metamodeling and flooding classification to perform fast prediction of unexplored input scenarios. It allows to obtain data distributions that reflect output uncertainty and to estimate variance-based sensitivity indices to quantify the influence of input uncertainty over output variability. Results show that uncertainty is strongly dependent on time and spatial location. Hydrograph-related parameters mainly control the timing and magnitude of the early flow, whereas yield stress becomes more influential in regions associated with flow attenuation, spreading and possible arrest. Overall, the framework provides probabilistic hazard estimates and insights into the physical mechanisms governing the dynamics of tailings flow.

authors.name: Yuri Taglieri S\'ao, Geraldo de Freitas Maciel, Julian Cardoso Eleut\'erio

papers.title: Stochastic Optimisation for Scalable Ptychographic Image Reconstruction
papers.summary: X-ray ptychography is a lensless coherent diffraction imaging technique capable of high spatial resolution, in which an image is reconstructed by solving a large-scale inverse problem from highly redundant far-field diffraction measurements acquired under overlapping illumination. Whilst the measurement redundancy created by overlapping illumination is essential for reconstruction fidelity, it leads to computational and memory demands that scale poorly with object size and target resolution when using conventional reconstruction algorithms. This work proposes a ptychographic reconstruction framework that reduces peak memory usage and time to convergence by leveraging stochastic optimisation techniques developed for large-scale machine learning. Specifically, the framework employs stochastic gradient descent with a decaying step size that progressively reduces the effect of gradient noise, referred to here as variance reduction (VR), with gradients that agree with automatic differentiation, to optimise the ptychographic forward model using randomly sampled subsets of diffraction measurements. For an experimental dataset of 200,000 diffraction patterns of $128\times128$ pixels, VR is demonstrated to require $65\%$ of the peak GPU memory and $22\%$ of the reconstruction time of the established maximum-likelihood (ML) algorithm. The VR framework incorporates the Poisson maximum-likelihood formulation and partial coherence within a unified and extensible optimisation setting. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the framework achieves reconstruction quality visually comparable to established methods, with lower peak GPU memory and a shorter time

authors.name: Alan W. Muriithi, Jared Tanner, Jaroslav M. Fowkes, Benedikt J. Daurer

papers.title: Neither graphs nor hypergraphs: structural moments of higher-order interactions determine stochastic social-impact dynamics
papers.summary: Whether higher-order interactions can be reduced to simpler representations is a question about the dynamics they drive, not only about their structure: what can be discarded is whatever the dynamics does not see. We make this precise for binary-state stochastic dynamics in which each agent, when updated, interacts with a randomly selected group and changes state according to the fraction of disagreeing members, as in generalized voter and social-impact models on hypergraphs. We ask which statistics of the group-interaction process determine the resulting Markov dynamics. For response functions that are polynomials of degree $q$, the answer is a hierarchy of size-weighted inclusion moments, which we call structural moments, involving at most $q$ neighbors at a time, regardless of how large the groups are. These moments are not only sufficient but also necessary: two interaction structures produce identical dynamics for all such rules if and only if their moments coincide. More generally, each class of rules selects its own minimal structural description, ranging from weighted pairwise links for linear rules to the full distribution of co-membership by group size for arbitrary rules. For voter-type rules, the same moments also reconstruct exact pairwise copying representations of these dynamics.

authors.name: Emanuele Cozzo

papers.title: In-memory measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution
papers.summary: Quantum memories offer to significantly extend the performance of quantum networks, but their complexity and limited performance at telecommunication wavelengths have so far hindered practical deployment. We propose a new memory-assisted measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol based on in-memory interference. Our approach leverages progress in atomic ensemble memories that enable the interference of a stationary matter qubit and a travelling photonic qubit inside a single quantum memory. We quantitatively evaluate the performance of this scheme against memoryless MDI-QKD and existing two-memory architectures, showing that it not only achieves superior secret key rates and surpasses the memoryless bound at substantially shorter distances, but also reduces hardware requirements by halving the number of memories and detectors. Our results further indicate that off resonant cascaded absorption (ORCA) memories are a particularly promising platform for implementing this protocol, and we outline a concrete design compatible with their capabilities. These findings demonstrate that in-memory interference provides a higher performance, and resource efficient route toward near term memory enhanced quantum secure communications.

authors.name: Nicolas Gauriot, Samuel Morrissey, Paul M. Burdekin, Ilse Maillette de Buy Wenniger, Sarah E. Thomas, Ian A. Walmsley, Robert I. Woodward, R. Mark Stevenson

papers.title: Numerical integration of non-local master equations for renewal shot noise with drift and state-dependent amplitude
papers.summary: The probability density of a system driven by a drift and a renewal train of kicks with state-dependent amplitude obeys a master equation that is non-local in space, because the kick operator $\hat{p}(i\partial_x I(x))$ is of infinite order, and, for non-exponential waiting times, non-local in time, with a memory kernel containing the propagator of the drift. Its solutions contain quasi-singular components, the never-kicked mass, which collapse onto the attractors of the drift. We present an accurate numerical method for such equations. The kick operator is a push-forward along the Marcus flow; in the Lamperti variable it becomes a translation, whose exact cell-to-cell weights follow from the cumulative distribution of the kicks, without quadrature. The drift is integrated by a conservative semi-Lagrangian step exact in time. The memory is represented by a sum of exponentials whose auxiliary fields are advected by the drift, at a cost linear in the number of steps. The never-kicked mass is transported exactly. For each ingredient we quantify the errors of simpler alternatives. The method is verified against exact solutions and event-driven Monte Carlo simulations with exact flow maps, from which it is statistically indistinguishable with $10^8$ trajectories. Parameters tuned for Gaussian kicks carry over unchanged to other kick distributions, and near a zero of the coupling, where the density vanishes faster than any power, the solution follows the known asymptotic law down to densities of order $10^{-37}$, far beyond Monte Carlo reach. As an application we compare the exact equation with its local and Poissonian approximations: in the range explored, the local equation deviates by up to 8% of the density width, also for waiting times with finite mean, consistently with an error estimate predicting larger deviations for slow drifts at long times. A Fortran implementation is available.

authors.name: Marco Bianucci, Riccardo Mannella

papers.title: OmniFish: A Bioinspired, Modular, Reconfigurable Soft Robotic Fish Enabling Multi-Modal Swimming
papers.summary: In this work, we introduce OmniFish, a bioinspired modular soft robotic fish designed to emulate the full spectrum of body and/or caudal fin (BCF) locomotion modes within a single robotic platform. The design combines morphology averaging across representative fish species with a tendon-driven compliant segmented spine whose effective stiffness can be reconfigured through progressive mechanical jamming. By selectively constraining body segments, OmniFish shifts deformation from whole-body undulation to posterior body bending and localized tail oscillation, enabling bioinspired Anguilliform, Subcarangiform, Carangiform, Thunniform, and Ostraciiform swimming using a single tendon-driven actuator. The design was guided by morphometric analysis and evaluated through caudal-fin thrust characterization, numerical body-drag simulations, kinematic analysis, and swimming performance experiments. Kinematic analysis confirmed the intended robot transition from distributed body undulation to localized tail oscillation. Swimming experiments demonstrated distinct mode-dependent performance, with the Ostraciiform configuration achieving the highest straight-line velocity of 8.14 cm/s and the lowest cost of transport of 2.42 at 1.5 tail beats/s. These proof-of-concept results show that a mechanically simple stiffness-reconfigurable architecture can generate distinct BCF swimming modes and provide a versatile strategy for developing multimodal soft robotic fish.

authors.name: Mathias Jensen, Saravana Prashanth Murali Babu

papers.title: Machine-learned potentials for iron oxides at extreme conditions
papers.summary: Reliable phase stability requires accurate relative free energies, which small force errors alone do not guarantee. We develop atomic-cluster-expansion potentials for five iron oxides from Fe$_2$O to Fe$_2$O$_3$, covering crystalline and liquid states at 140--260\,GPa and 1000--11000\,K, with electronic and ionic temperatures matched. Force-dominated training leaves systematic energy offsets between structure families of up to 41\,meV/atom that persist despite additional training data. Stronger energy weighting and weaker regularization largely remove these offsets, while converged k-point sampling prevents further composition-dependent biases. The final potentials achieve held-out energy errors of 2.0--5.5\,meV/atom and first-order free-energy errors within 3.4\,meV/atom for liquids at 5000--9000\,K. However, an untrained NiAs-type FeO phase exhibits a free-energy error of 57\,meV/atom despite a low extrapolation grade. These results show that reliable phase-diagram calculations require control of relative energy offsets and explicit free-energy validation of every competing phase.

authors.name: S. Azadi, S. M. Vinko, T. D. K\"{u}hne, A. Principi, M. S. Bahramy

papers.title: Reliable arithmetic circuits using less reliable (sub-digital) logic
