Bounds under assumed differences in spike detection connect recorded rates to biological rate changes. We assess recording loss and uncertainty in rate changes in simulations, and count-model fit in recordings. We also compare two transformer estimators with Gaussian and flow variational inference under a shared temporal negative-binomial model. Flow variational inference agrees most closely with reference posteriors, while predictive performance varies across mice. Rate-change intervals contain true simulated changes less often than intended. In UnitMatch recordings from five mice, some inferred changes remain supported when spike detection is allowed to differ between days; others depend on equal detection. These interpretations require a correct neuron match. The approach identifies which inferred rate changes remain supported under specified recording assumptions and where uncertainty limits interpretation.

authors.name: Nilson Chapagain, Pooja Chapagain

papers.title: Digital Twin Models for Malaria Transmission: A Classical and Stieltjes Derivative Approach
papers.summary: We propose two mathematical models for malaria transmission grounded in mosquito--human interactions and the digital twin framework. The first model is formulated using classical derivatives, whereas the second employs Stieltjes derivatives to represent abrupt biological events such as egg hatching and adult-emergence pulses in \emph{Anopheles} mosquito populations. The Stieltjes formulation unifies, in a single equation with two derivators, the continuous transmission dynamics, the biological impulses and the data-assimilation corrections of the digital twin; we prove its well-posedness, specify the order of biological and assimilation atoms when they coincide, and give quantitative conditions under which additive emergence pulses preserve biological admissibility. The numerical study uses 132 monthly confirmed-malaria observations from Kebbi State (January 2015--December 2025) and a synthetic entomological series generated in a controlled recovery experiment, because no measured mosquito time series is available. Parameters are updated incrementally on rolling windows, and one-step-ahead forecasts combine the mechanistic ensemble with a past-only seasonal-persistence component. In the recovery experiment, the model endowed with seasonal recruitment and emergence pulses, which the Stieltjes derivator represents exactly, recovers the synthetic vector dynamics far better than the unforced classical model; this gain is attributable to the seasonal and impulsive mechanisms rather than to the derivative calculus itself, and the phase and pulse schedule of the generator were known to the model. The human-case results are comparable between both formulations; the one-step forecasts improve on a seasonal-naive predictor but not on last-month persistence, so they must be interpreted as a proof of concept rather than as an independent epidemiological validation.

authors.name: Iv\'an Area, Emmanuel Afolabi Bakare, Francisco J. Fern\'andez, Daniel Muyiwa Adefisoye

papers.title: Structure-Preserving Universal Differential Equations for Epidemic Dynamics
papers.summary: Universal differential equations (UDEs) combine mechanistic epidemic models with learned neural closures, but generic additive corrections may violate essential epidemiological properties. We introduce a class of structure-preserving epidemic UDEs in which learned closures parameterize intercompartmental fluxes and the force of infection factorizes through infected compartments. This architecture guarantees positivity, population boundedness, and invariance of the disease-free set. We derive a rank-one next-generation matrix and a closed-form basic reproduction number determined by the learned rates at the disease-free equilibrium. Under explicit conditions, we establish results on threshold dynamics, disease-free and endemic equilibria, stability, and uniform persistence. For a neural SEIR model, center manifold analysis characterizes the direction of bifurcation through derivatives of the learned transmission rate. We further establish fundamental identifiability limitations: closures that agree on observed epidemic trajectories can yield different reproduction numbers and bifurcation types. Quantitative bounds relate uncertainty in the reproduction number to closure regularity and the distance of observations from the disease-free equilibrium, while monotonicity provides one-sided bounds. A numerical example involving three closures illustrates these results. Our findings provide a rigorous framework for epidemiologically consistent scientific machine learning and clarify which dynamical properties can be recovered from epidemic data.

authors.name: ABdallah Alsammani, Maia Martcheva

papers.title: Benchmarking Traditional and Learning-Based Reference-Free Compressors for Long-Read Sequencing Data
papers.summary: Long-read sequencing technologies generate large volumes of data, creating substantial storage and transmission demands. Although reference-based compressors can achieve high compression, their reliance on an appropriate reference genome limits their use. We present LRCBench, a benchmark and survey of reference-free lossless compressors for long-read sequencing data. We review traditional and learning-based general-purpose and sequencing-specific methods, then evaluate 35 compressors on 16 real-world datasets from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio platforms. We compare compression ratio, storage savings, runtime, peak memory use, and robustness across datasets. Learning-based compressors are evaluated on six MinION datasets because of their high computational costs. CoLoRd achieves the best overall compression ratios in our experiments, while other methods offer trade-offs in speed, memory use, and robustness. We also examine multithreaded speedup and discuss future directions in parallel acceleration, privacy protection, adaptive parameter tuning, and hardware-algorithm co-design.

authors.name: Huidong Ma, Hui Sun, Xinyan Shi, Cheng Zhong, Xiaoguang Liu, Gang Wang

papers.title: Micrograph B-factor estimation via Wilson statistics
papers.summary: The single-particle cryo-electron microscopy imaging process is known to cause exponential decay in the amplitude and power spectra of proteins. This decay is modeled by the B factor and is currently corrected as a post-processing stage of the 3D reconstruction. As a consequence, all experimental images in the dataset are assumed to share the same B factor. In this paper, we suggest a novel approach wherein the B factor is determined and corrected as a preprocessing step to the reconstruction. We show such an approach can improve reconstruction resolution.

authors.name: Ayelet Heimowitz, Amit Singer

papers.title: Old Matches, New Frames: Schedule-Gated Stereo Memory from Human Vision to Machine Matching
papers.summary: Human vision and video stereo networks both reuse disparity evidence across time, yet a refresh of the input can invalidate a match formed milliseconds earlier. What tells a system whether an old match still counts? We answer this from limited human data in three steps. First, nine temporal mechanisms share a frozen binocular-energy front end and an equal-capacity readout, so held-out behavior isolates the temporal selection rule: on 240 conditions from 10 observers, down-weighting aged evidence that has lost binocular support lowers subject RMSE from 12.6% to 10.3% and reproduces a period-dependent reversed-depth illusion, across all 59 readings of the unpublished protocol and 8 front-end perturbations. Second, four propositions establish what such data can identify: gating is identified at the level of the refresh schedule, and candidate binding is invisible to standard stimuli but exposed by a single-eye geometry flip that separates the readouts by up to 7.1%. Third, the identified rule becomes a two-field stereo memory that separates sample validity from hypothesis support. It removes a 50 ms recovery lag after geometry flips, and its regime analysis explains why plain integration stays preferable on MPI-Sintel, where 71.1% of pixels change appearance but not disparity.

authors.name: Ruiqi Liu, Yang Lu, Yanlan Kang

papers.title: A multiscale discrete-to-continuum framework for structured population models
papers.summary: Mathematical models of biological populations commonly use discrete structure classes to capture trait variation among individuals (e.g. age, size, phenotype, intracellular state). Upscaling these discrete models into continuum descriptions can improve analytical tractability and scalability of numerical solutions. Common upscaling approaches based solely on Taylor expansions may, however, introduce ambiguities in truncation order, uniform validity and boundary conditions. To address this, here we introduce a discrete multiscale framework to systematically derive continuum approximations of structured population models. Using the method of multiple scales and matched asymptotic expansions applied to discrete systems, we identify regions of structure space for which a continuum representation is appropriate and derive the corresponding partial differential equations. The leading-order dynamics are given by an advection equation in the bulk domain and advection-diffusion processes in small inner layers about wavefronts. We further derive discrete boundary layer descriptions for regions where the discrete model cannot be approximated by a continuum description. Finally, we demonstrate the method on a simple lipid-structured model for early atherosclerosis and verify consistency between the discrete and continuum descriptions. The multiscale framework we present can be applied to other heterogeneous systems with discrete structure in order to obtain appropriate upscaled dynamics with asymptotically consistent boundary conditions.

authors.name: Eleonora Agostinelli, Keith L. Chambers, Helen M. Byrne, Mohit P. Dalwadi

papers.title: Persistent Homology as a Morphological Signature of Fibrin Networks
papers.summary: We present an investigation of the applicability of topological data analysis (TDA) to the study of high-resolution confocal microscopy images of fibrin network structures from patients with oesophageal cancer undergoing intended curative surgery. Investigation of clot structure brings new knowledge about blood coagulation, risk of bleeding, and thrombosis in this group of patients. Images of fibrin network formation in the collected blood samples were captured by confocal microscopy and three-dimensional z-stacks were analysed. Each z-stack was cropped to a centre region for analysis, the validity of which is assessed in detail. Overall, we found no significant differences in fibrin network topology across the perioperative period, and no consistent differences in network structure between the standard and intervention groups.

authors.name: Thomas Burnett, Theresa Reinhold, Bea Bleile, Sophie Raynor, Freya Jensen, Martin Hermann, Tua Gyldenholm, Yossi Bokor Bleile

papers.title: An information-geometric framework for mapping maximum potential biodiversity
papers.summary: Biodiversity measures are often used descriptively: one computes a diversity index from an observed or estimated community composition and maps the resulting values across space. Conservation planning, however, also requires a site-specific benchmark against which the observed community can be compared. This chapter develops an information-geometric framework for such \emph{potential diversity} and the associated \emph{diversity gap}. The central object is a pair of probability vectors on the species simplex: an observed or realized composition \(p^{\mathrm{obs}}\), and a potential composition \(p^{\mathrm{pot}}\) obtained by a constrained variational principle. The gap is then defined by comparing a diversity functional at these two compositions. The framework is developed for both Hill-type diversity, which measures abundance and evenness, and Rao's quadratic entropy, which incorporates trait, phylogenetic, or ecological dissimilarities among species. A spatial point-process interpretation clarifies how local ecological capacities can be defined before passing to the simplex. Escort constraints, capacity constraints, and divergence projections then provide a unified way to define nontrivial benchmarks beyond the uniform distribution. The resulting formulation separates two distinct questions: how diverse a community is, and how far it is from a locally admissible potential benchmark. It also connects the ecological idea of dark diversity with a continuous, abundance-weighted comparison on the probability simplex. We also outline a dynamic extension in which capacities, species migration, and climate-driven shifts vary over time. Empirical implementation with large-scale citizen-science biodiversity data and trait databases is left for future work.

authors.name: Shinto Eguchi

papers.title: The Bapat-Sunder eigenvalue conjecture fails over the reals
papers.summary: In 1986 Bapat and Sunder asked whether $\operatorname{per}(A)$ is the largest eigenvalue of $F_A=[a_{i,j}\operatorname{per}(A(i,j))]$ for every positive semidefinite Hermitian $A$, where $A(i,j)$ deletes row $i$ and column $j$. Drury disproved this over the complex field in 2018 and conjectured that the property holds for real positive semidefinite matrices. We disprove Drury's conjecture with a rank-$4$, $32\times32$ integer Gram matrix and an integer vector whose Rayleigh quotient exceeds $\operatorname{per}(A)$; verification uses integer arithmetic. Together, the two counterexamples resolve the Bapat-Sunder eigenvalue conjecture negatively over both fields. Counterexamples exist of every order $n\ge32$. As an application to quantum optics, the violation yields a $36$-mode orthogonal interferometer and a direction of relative arrival-time delays among $32$ photons with identical-variance Gaussian wave packets along which every sufficiently small nonzero delay increases the probability that all photons are detected within four designated output modes.

authors.name: Logan R. Chalmers

papers.title: Scrambling leads to entanglement cost in NLQC
papers.summary: In a non-local quantum computation (NLQC), shared entanglement along with a single simultaneous round of quantum communication is used to implement a joint channel. NLQC has many applications, most of which benefit from an understanding of lower bounds on the entanglement needed to implement a given channel as an NLQC. However, the properties of a channel that lead to it having an entanglement cost in NLQC have remained unclear, with most lower bounds only applying to specially constructed examples. Here, we give a new lower bound technique for unitaries based on scrambling: we find that a unitary has zero entanglement cost if and only if it does not scramble. Further, we find that the tripartite mutual information, an entropic object that quantifies the degree of scrambling, provides a quantitative lower bound on entanglement cost in NLQC. This is the first known lower bound on entanglement cost for unitaries in NLQC which is faithful. Our results also relate scrambling and NLQC for the first time. Leveraging the faithful scrambling based bound, we then show that the controllable correlation, an earlier studied quantity, is also a faithful lower bound, resolving an earlier conjecture of Cleve and May.

authors.name: Atsuya Hasegawa, Alex May

papers.title: Look Mum, No Hands! Quantum State Preparation without Time-Dependent Control
papers.summary: How much can be prepared with a quantum system whose Hamiltonian cannot be modulated in time? Common intuition suggests that the answer is not much. Without a knob to turn during the evolution, a system seems confined to a fixed trajectory through its state space, while time-dependent control can steer it almost anywhere. We put this intuition to the test by studying autonomous control, i.e., state preparation with a time-invariant Hamiltonian, where the only freedom lies in the static coupling strengths and the evolution time. We characterize basic mathematical properties of the autonomously reachable set and introduce two criteria of unreachability: a certificate that is cheap to evaluate and rigorously excludes that a target state can be reached for any choice of control parameters, and a stronger criterion based on exhaustive numerical optimization. With these tools we estimate the probability that a typical state in Hilbert space is unreachable under randomly drawn control terms. The dimensionality of the reachable set turns out to be independent of the system, yet the fraction of Hilbert space lying close to it depends strongly on the choice of control Hamiltonians. Strikingly, for sufficiently random controls and long enough evolution times, almost every state can become approximately reachable, even with the fewest generators that permit full controllability with time-dependent couplings. Autonomous control can approach the expressivity of time-dependent control, at the cost of longer evolution times.

authors.name: Tomasz Andrzejewski, Yuri Minoguchi, Phila Rembold, Konrad Szyma\'nski

papers.title: Optimal Joint Bounds for Sparse Ground-State Energy Estimation and Ground-State Preparation
papers.summary: Ground-state energy estimation (GSEE) and ground-state preparation (GSP) are fundamental problems in quantum computing. Given a Hamiltonian $H$ with $\|H\|\le1$ and a guiding state $|\psi\rangle$ with overlap at least $\gamma>0$ with the ground space of $H$, the goal in GSEE is to estimate the ground-state energy of $H$ to additive error $\delta$ with failure probability at most $\varepsilon$, while in GSP it is to prepare a state with ground-space weight at least $1-\varepsilon$, given a gap lower bound $\Delta$. Their costs are measured by quantum query complexity, i.e., the number of oracle calls needed to access $H$. Recent work proved optimal bounds $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\delta))$ for GSEE and $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\Delta))$ for GSP in the time-evolution and block-encoding models. However, these models do not directly account for the sparsity of $H$, measured by the maximum number $s$ of nonzero entries in any row or column. In the sparse-access model, oracles instead return the locations and values of these entries. This introduces the additional parameter $s$, and it remained open how query complexity depends jointly on $s$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ or $\Delta$, and $\varepsilon$. We resolve this by proving sparse-query lower bounds $\Omega(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\delta))$ for GSEE and $\Omega(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\Delta))$ for GSP, even for stoquastic Hamiltonians. We also show that these constructions recover the earlier time-evolution and block-encoding lower-bound scalings. We then give matching upper-bound algorithms in the reversible in-place sparse-location model. Thus, we obtain $\Theta(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\delta))$ for GSEE and $\Theta(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\Delta))$ for GSP, showing that $\sqrt{s}$ is necessary and sufficient and completing the joint dependence on all problem parameters.

authors.name: Dhrumil Patel

papers.title: Qubit-qumode simulation of molecular torsion in photoisomerization
papers.summary: Photochemical reactions driven by large nuclear motion, such as the photoisomerization of retinal, depend strongly on both the global anharmonic forces of the potential and the periodic topology of molecular torsion. In this work, we develop a hybrid discrete (qubit) and continuous variable (qumode) quantum simulation framework for photochemical reactions that maps electronic states to qubits, vibrations to qumodes, and the periodic torsion to a compact qumode encoding. Applying this approach to the two-mode Hahn-Stock and three-mode PSB3 models of retinal photoisomerization, we compare i) local vibronic approximations, ii) the full trigonometric potential on the noncompact line, and iii) the same potential on the compact circle, which matches the molecular torsion topology. We numerically show that the topological description can significantly alter relevant observables. We realize the compact torsion via both a wrapped Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) encoding and a two-qumode circle encoding and introduce two methods that reduce the hardware resources of both encodings. Spreading an encoded coordinate over several qumodes lowers the average occupation number of each mode, and adding counterterms to the Hamiltonian reduces the required squeezing amount. We expect that these methods make percent-level simulations of the considered molecules promising targets for hybrid qubit-qumode hardware. For more complex molecules, each additional nuclear coordinate is represented directly as a single qumode or an encoded register using the same native operations, so the framework extends naturally to larger systems.

authors.name: Dimitrios Athanasakos, Florian Hechenberger, Tommaso Rainaldi, Felix Ringer, George Siopsis

papers.title: Experimental constraints on gauge hidden-variable models in Bell tests
papers.summary: Quantum mechanics assigns identical statistics to measurement procedures that realize the same final effect, irrespective of the transformations used to reach it. We test this operational equivalence with polarization-entangled photons by implementing one of Bob's analyzer settings either directly or through closed wave-plate trajectories $C_\gamma$ calibrated to produce the same measurement operator. Motivated by ontological descriptions in which a hidden frame is transported between contexts, we formulate a local path-memory model and derive the mixed-context bound $|S_\gamma^{\rm mix}|\leq 2+2p_\gamma$. The quantity $p_\gamma$ is a coupling-dependent counterfactual mismatch probability: it bounds a contextual Bell expression, but neither generates nor predicts the quantum Bell correlation. We therefore test path memory through the observable difference between direct and looped implementations, using a no-signaling phenomenological response in which a hidden holonomy $\delta_\gamma$ modifies one correlation term in $S_\gamma^{\rm mix}$. The direct reference violates the Bell inequality, while the looped mixed-context curves remain indistinguishable from it within the experimental precision. Our results support the quantum equivalence of calibrated measurement implementations and constrain path-sensitive hidden-variable extensions that predict an observable memory of the optical history.

authors.name: Li-Yu Shen, Lukas Scarfe, Carrie Rodriguez, Alessio D'Errico, Andrea Aiello, Ebrahim Karimi

papers.title: High-rate low-distance color codes
papers.summary: Experimental implementations of two-dimensional color codes encoding a single logical qubit have surpassed the fidelity of physical qubits. A natural next step is to investigate higher-rate codes that encode multiple logical qubits. Here we propose small, high-rate 2D color codes for this purpose. We design distance-$3$ codes with encoding rates up to $1/3$ and distance-$4$ codes with encoding rates up to $1/4$. We prove that these rates are optimal for color codes with only color boundaries on surfaces with non-negative Euler characteristic. We benchmark the codes by simulating Steane-style error correction with real-time feedback and no post-selection in a linear trapped-ion chain model with all-to-all connectivity. The two best-performing codes have parameters $[[20,4,4]]$ and $[[16,4,4]]$ and achieve break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of $0.22\%$ and $0.26\%$, respectively. These results match the performance of Shor-style error correction with bivariate bicycle codes that use weight-$5$ measurements.

authors.name: Peter-Jan H. S. Derks, Lucas Berent, Mark Webster, Robert Wille, Jens Eisert, Aleksander Kubica

papers.title: Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing for Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout
papers.summary: We introduce DIRAC, an ADC-less in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that uses analog computing to redraw the analog-digital boundary. Directly operating on the front-end's analog output, passive complex mixers perform the equivalent of digital demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators average their outputs into down-sampled per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes them, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives the mixers' local oscillators from the readout transmitter's baseband rather than per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration flow trains the matched filter jointly with the neural network, improving fidelity and enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, DIRAC matches the fidelity of a floating-point (FP32) digital pipeline for readout windows down to 750 ns, at 31.6$\times$ and 238$\times$ lower energy than the fixed-point (FxP) and FP32 pipelines. It cuts the total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% relative to FxP and room-temperature flex cables, respectively. At a fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, this yields, against FxP, a code distance larger by 2 to 6 and a 1.6-7.3$\times$ (Willow) and 4.9-204$\times$ (SI1000, $p = 10^{-3}$) lower logical error rate.

authors.name: Qirui Zhang, Ben Toby, He Wang, Benjamin Lienhard, David Blaauw, Dennis Sylvester

papers.title: QCCDCert: Formally Verified Compilation for QCCD Co-Design
papers.summary: Quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architectures enable scalable trapped-ion quantum computing by dynamically shuttling ions between specialized processing and storage zones. A QCCD can be built with many trap sizes and layouts. Comparing them requires compiling every program under each design's transport, capacity and control constraints, and trusting the target code of each compilation. We present a co-design framework built on one Lean-verified compiler. The hardware description and its operating rules are compiler inputs, so a single theorem covers every candidate design: the target code of every compilation preserves its program's behavior and obeys the hardware rules. Across 75 benchmark programs of 11 to 130 qubits, the best design found takes 66% less modeled execution time on average than the worst design of equal capacity. An AI agent that proposes devices based on our compiler's checked results beats the fastest of these designs on 71 of 75 programs. Our verified compiler provably avoids the 11 defects that we report in three previous compilers. It scales to hundreds of qubits, compiling 512-qubit programs for a 38-trap device in 1 to 29 minutes.

authors.name: John Zhuoyang Ye, Jens Palsberg, Ke Sun, Hartmut Haeffner

papers.title: Degree and normalization frontiers for bounded QSVT inversion
papers.summary: Quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) implements matrix inversion using bounded polynomials. Increasing polynomial degree can improve normalization and reduce amplified query cost, with savings that depend on the error criterion. However, existing bounded methods either fix the normalization or work far below the condition numbers of fault-tolerant resource estimates. We therefore analyze this trade-off for absolute reciprocal error, which controls inverse-operator accuracy, and for residual error, which suffices for normalized linear solves. For absolute reciprocal error, we establish a scaling limit to a constrained least-norm problem for entire functions and characterize its high-accuracy frontier using elliptic integrals. Constructions built from near-optimal limiting functions achieve certified query-cost savings over the rescaled minimax baseline of at least 11.8 percent at condition number ten thousand with error one millionth, and at least 22.8 percent at one million with error one ten-billionth. A simpler two-term rule also has certified savings, and its phase factors at condition number ten thousand pass numerical checks at selected points. For residual error, a sparse Chebyshev construction achieves certified savings over the residual-minimax baseline of at least 8.7 percent at condition number ten thousand with normalized-state error at most one hundred-millionth, and at least 13.1 percent at one million with error at most one ten-billionth. These results quantify the saving that a joint choice of degree and normalization gives beyond the minimax baselines.

authors.name: Hongyu Wu

papers.title: Quantum resources and the onset of the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem
papers.summary: The Monte Carlo sign problem poses a fundamental obstacle to classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, yet its connection to quantum resources remains poorly understood. We probe this connection by systematically tuning the degree of nonstoquasticity in random k-local Hamiltonians. In numerical tensor-network studies, we find the sign complexity and the quantum resources of entanglement and nonstabilizerness of the ground state to be strongly suppressed in a broad regime up to substantial nonstoquasticity. As nonstoquasticity is further increased, the considered quantum resources experience sharp crossovers into a regime where they are strongly enhanced. Surprisingly, numerical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations drastically deteriorate in the same region, even though the Hamiltonian is already considerably nonstoquastic well before it, indicating that the failure of ground-state QMC is correlated more with the resource content of the state than the sign structure of the Hamiltonian. We corroborate these findings analytically by constructing an approximate ground state of k-local Hamiltonians in the stoquastic limit. Moreover, we identify a distinct behaviour in graph states. Their nonstabilizerness always vanishes, but, as we demonstrate analytically, on bipartite graphs the sign can be easily cured while in multipartite graph states it cannot. Our results thus shed light on the highly subtle interplay between quantum resources and the computational difficulty encountered by QMC methods.

authors.name: Naga Dileep Varikuti, Leela Ganesh Chandra Lakkaraju, Philipp Hauke

papers.title: Singlet flags: using native entanglement to restore the circuit distance of shuttled qLDPC codes in silicon
papers.summary: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes could greatly reduce the qubit count of silicon spin-qubit processors, but their checks are long-range and of high weight. Shuttling one ancilla electron through every data qubit of a check measures such checks, but a single fault on the ancilla spreads to several data qubits, so the circuit distance can fall far below the code distance. We make the mobile ancilla one half of a spin singlet whose partner stays at home; a Bell measurement at the end of the check provides a flag for isolated bit-flip faults acquired during the walk. Using new distance-6 codes with check weights 8, 10 and 12, and exact circuit distances from two independent solvers, we show that without the flag the circuit distance falls as check weight grows, to 1 at weight 12, while with it every weight-8 and weight-10 code recovers circuit distance 5 or 6 and corrects as many faults as the code. For codes of distance 8 to 12 the flag raises the circuit distance by one to four, and the Gross code [[144,12,12]] rises from 7 to 10. In circuit-level simulations of shuttled spin qubits, the flag lowers logical error rates by typically 2-10x across bivariate-bicycle, circulant-permutation and surface codes, and the gain survives percent-level flag-readout errors and bit flips on the singlet's electrons. BP+OSD does not reach the full circuit distance of the flagged circuits, so our flagged logical error rates are upper bounds: decoding the same shots exactly raises the flag's gain on the distance-6 codes from 3-7x to 5-17x for the weight-6 BB code, and from 1-12x to 5-90x at weights 8 and 10 for p >= 2.5x10^-4.

authors.name: William Chow, Jonathan Baugh

papers.title: Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite Qubit System
papers.summary: Quantum Computing uses quantum mechanical phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement of quantum bits (qubits), to represent and manipulate information in multidimensional state spaces. This approach allows complex mathematical functions to be executed simultaneously rather than sequentially, making them much more efficient than classical computers. However, current quantum computers suffer from quantum decoherence, where small changes to their environment, such as thermal fluctuations and vibrations, affect the systems' fragile states. The goal of this study is to discuss the functionality of a proposed Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite qubit system by solving the unitary time-evolution of a quantum state vector for the system's Hamiltonian, using known axial and traverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K. The system can effectively transfer population between its two lowest states at rates predicted by the Rabi half-period, with 99.9% fidelity. Additionally, it can hold the population at a desired state without docohering. The results remained consistent for temperatures up to 10 K, meaning, unlike many common qubit systems, the proposed qubit system could function without a dilution fridge and is not fragile to thermal noise.

authors.name: Dishaanth S. Pillai, G. M. Wysin

papers.title: Spectral Disks for Quantum Markov Generators
papers.summary: Spectral bounds for Markov generators require a choice of time scale. In quantum dynamics, a rate read off from a jump representation, the escape rate from a pure state and the smallest spectral disk need not agree. We prove that the spectrum of every GKLS generator written without a Hamiltonian lies in a disk tangent to the imaginary axis, with radius given by the norm of the operator $\Phi^\dagger(I)$ built from the jump map $\Phi$. This settles the first two scaling conjectures of "Corralling spectra of generators of time-continuous Markov evolution (both classical and quantum)", J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. {59}, 175202 (2026). The third, escape-rate conjecture fails for a qutrit with a single normal jump. Nevertheless, twice the escape rate bounds every decay rate of any positive trace-preserving semigroup For GKLS generators with vanishing canonical Hamiltonian, four times the escape rate always supplies a spectral disk, and the factor four is optimal uniformly in dimension. We compare these bounds with classical Cassini ovals and thermodynamic ellipses, explain the obstacles to their quantum extensions, and formulate optimization over completely positive jump-map representations as a semidefinite program.

authors.name: Dariusz Chru\'sci\'nski, Sergey Denisov, Wojciech Tarnowski, Karol \.Zyczkowski

papers.title: Instrument indeterminacy: separating uncertainty in POVM effects and its neutrosophic reading
papers.summary: Neutrosophic annotation frameworks for quantum measurement attach an external triple $(t,i,f)$ to each Born probability, and explicitly leave open how indeterminacy could be defined operationally. We show that indeterminacy cannot be recovered from outcome probabilities, but can be computed from the pair (state, effect). For a binary POVM $\{A, I-A\}$ we define the instrument indeterminacy $\mathcal{I}_\rho(A) = 4 \mathrm{Tr}(\rho(A-A^2))$, which vanishes exactly when the state only sees the sharp part of the effect. The normalized Gini index of the outcome splits as $4TF = \mathcal{I}_\rho(A) + 4 \mathrm{Var}_\rho(A)$, a law of total variance that separates the instrument contribution from the state contribution; the identity is a special case of Massar's POVM uncertainty operator, and our contribution is its neutrosophic reading. Moving the system-apparatus cut to a Naimark dilation transfers exactly $\mathcal{I}_\rho(A)$ from indeterminacy to variance, which yields the missing operational definition. We extend the decomposition to $m$-outcome POVMs, relate the minimum indeterminacy of two incompatible unbiased qubit observables to their commutator through Busch's joint-measurability criterion, and show that $\mathcal{I}_\rho(A)$ equals twice the disagreement probability of a repeated L\"uders measurement. The resulting estimator needs neither the state nor the effect and, in simulation, requires 2.5 to 6 times fewer shots than detector tomography for the same error.

authors.name: Fernando A. Otero

papers.title: Perspectives on the hidden subgroup problem over unitriangular groups
papers.summary: We investigate the quantum Hidden Subgroup Problem (HSP) over the upper unitriangular group $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$. While efficient quantum algorithms were discovered for some families of non abelian groups and nil-2 $p$-groups, no efficient algorithms are known for groups of nilpotency class higher than 2. The only techniques known for such groups scale exponentially in the size of the input. We first study the group $U_4(\mathbb{F}_p)$, the smallest upper unitriangular group exhibiting nilpotency class three. We analyze the application of the Pretty Good Measurement approach used for Heisenberg groups and show its limits. We then focus on the more general case $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$ to adapt existing techniques to this particular structure. In particular, we derive an algorithm for cyclic subgroups as a subroutine for a general algorithm, although it is not efficient in the size of the group. Our results highlight the difficulties introduced by the increasing nilpotency class and suggests some directions for an efficient quantum algorithm for the HSP over $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$.

authors.name: Damien Poquillon

papers.title: Uniformly Convergent Perturbation Theory for Open Quantum Systems at, near, and away from Exceptional Points
papers.summary: Near a Liouvillian exceptional point, spectral perturbation theory becomes ill-conditioned, yet the observable dynamics of a finite-dimensional open system remains regular in the perturbation. Using a Dyson expansion, which requires no diagonalization of the perturbed generator, we analyze the scaling, stability, and convergence of the perturbative corrections at, near and away from exceptional points. We derive scaling laws showing that nonperipheral Jordan blocks raise the degree of the polynomial-in-time factors multiplying decaying exponentials, which are present for any generator as resonances, and we quantify this excess. We further establish a uniform-in-time error estimate for the perturbative series, valid for any relaxing finite-dimensional Lindbladian and controlled by a parameter $q = |\varepsilon|R$, where $\varepsilon$ is the perturbation strength and $R$ is a constant built from unperturbed data. All constants of the bound remain continuous through an exceptional point when the coalescing eigenvalues are kept in one spectral cluster. The estimate extends to the frequency domain via the Laplace transform, and to time-dependent perturbations. We test it in a driven two-level system with a Liouvillian exceptional point, including perturbations that break its symmetry.

authors.name: Pedro Linck

papers.title: Parisi Energy before Parisi Geometry in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
papers.summary: The fractured low-energy landscape of spin glasses presents a notorious barrier to optimization. While high-depth calculations indicate that the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can approach the Parisi ground-state energy of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, how it does so remains elusive. Here, we treat the QAOA distribution as a statistical-physics object and probe its geometry directly in the thermodynamic limit. We draw two independent bitstrings from the same problem instance and couple them through their macroscopic similarity. We find that typical QAOA samples remain macroscopically uncorrelated, even as their sensitivity to this coupling grows with circuit depth $p$. By contrast, the low-energy tail shows a much stronger tendency to overlap and reveals a Parisi-like phase with the same critical behavior as the thermal spin-glass transition. The onset of this organization moves toward the typical output as the circuit deepens, consistent with the separation vanishing only as $p\to\infty$. Together, these findings suggest a route distinct from structure-exploiting classical algorithms and thermal sampling, one in which the QAOA approaches the Parisi energy before Parisi geometry becomes typical.

authors.name: Maxime Dupont, Bhuvanesh Sundar

papers.title: Renormalization and exact Bloch bands: the trigonometric Rosen-Morse model
papers.summary: We study the trigonometric Rosen-Morse potential as an isolated singular well and as an exactly solvable periodic lattice. The potential combines inverse-square singularities with Coulomb terms of opposite signs. In the strongly attractive regime, independent renormalization at the two endpoints gives a two-parameter family of spectra. Deep negative-energy levels form two asymptotic sequences with the same Efimov-like scaling and opposite first-order Coulomb corrections. In the weak-medium regime, self-adjoint matching conditions allow transmission between neighboring cells. We obtain the exact Bloch dispersion relation and determine the band widths, gaps, and electron and hole effective masses. At fixed band index, the bandwidth becomes exponentially small in the limit of large Coulomb coupling.

authors.name: Ulysses Camara da Silva, H. G. Vianna

papers.title: Separating QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy via a Switching Lemma for Polynomials
papers.summary: We construct a classical oracle relative to which QMA is not contained in the QCMA hierarchy. Our main technical contribution is a switching lemma for bounded polynomials, which provides a new conceptual viewpoint on earlier sampler-based arguments separating QMA and QCMA. Crucially, the parameters of this switching lemma are independent of the number of input variables. The separation builds on the code intersection subset size problem of Bostanci, Huang, and Vaikuntanathan (FOCS 2026). We also construct a classical oracle relative to which QCMA collapses to P but QMA does not, and another relative to which QMA collapses to P but PP does not.

authors.name: Yiming Wang

papers.title: Chirp-stabilized charging of a two-level quantum battery
papers.summary: Resonantly driven two-level quantum batteries (QBs) suffer from strong pulse-area dependence and energy backflow inherent to Rabi oscillations. To address this limitation, we propose charging of a two-level QB with chirped pulses. We investigate four charging protocols formed by pairing hyperbolic secant (sech) or Gaussian pulse envelopes with linear or hyperbolic-tangent (tanh) frequency sweeps. We show that sufficiently strong chirp modulation converts the charging mechanism from pulse-area-governed Rabi rotation to adiabatic rapid passage. We analyze the underlying adiabatic dynamics and derive the criteria for robust chirped charging, which incorporate the sweep bandwidth, nonadiabatic transitions, and dissipative effects. Under strong chirp modulation, the final stored energy and ergotropy converge to stable plateaus that are nearly insensitive to the pulse area across an extended parameter window. Of the four schemes, the sech pulse with tanh chirp delivers the widest ergotropy plateau and the weakest pulse area sensitivity. Compared with counterdiabatic driving, the sech tanh protocol attains stable charging performance without demanding an extra drive quadrature. Furthermore, this chirp-enabled charging is resilient to static detuning and weak-to-moderate dissipation. This work establishes a practical route toward robust charging of quantum batteries using chirped pulse control.

authors.name: Yang-Yang Yuan, Xian-Li Yin, Jin-Feng Huang, Jie-Qiao Liao

papers.title: Hierarchical coupling in tripartite van der Waals cavity magnonics for a low-loss and tunable coupled-mode Hamiltonian
papers.summary: One of the greatest merits of cavity magnonics (CM) is the ability to explore rich coupled-mode physics, driven by the large \textit{in situ} flux tunability of magnonic resonances and magnon--photon coupling. Meanwhile, van der Waals (vdW) magnets offer an ultra-compact and highly integrated implementation of CM without complex fabrication processes. Nonetheless, the substantial magnon losses significantly hinder the combination of all these advantages. Here, we realize a hierarchical anti-crossing structure in a tripartite vdW CM with CrCl3 and realize an effective coupled-dual-mode Hamiltonian. We achieve an order-of-magnitude reduction in loss while maintaining a strong coupling condition. Additionally, we theoretically confirm the feasibility of simultaneous and \textit{in situ} tuning of both loss and coupling by varying the magnetic field direction and strength. Featuring a micrometer-scale thickness and a width of a few millimeters, our device is significantly smaller than those based on bulk crystals or crystal arrays. Our results establish vdW cavity magnonics as versatile platform for investigating intriguing phenomena predicted in coupled-mode systems.

authors.name: Taehee Kim, Sunghun Park, Byoung-moo Ann, Sung Jin An, Seung-Bo Shim, Hakseong Kim, Haydar Sahin, Zhuo Bin Siu, Mansoor B. A. Jalil, Youngwook Kim, Thomas K. M. Graham, Brian B. Zhou, Myung-Joong Hwang, Yaroslav M. Blanter, Jungpil Seo, Hee Chul Park, Minkyung Jung

papers.title: Parity Push Post-Selection with Soft Parity Constraints for Quantum LDPC Codes
papers.summary: Post-selection lowers the logical error rate of a quantum error-correcting code by rejecting unreliable shots. For a code with $K$ logical observables, the logical gap, a standard post-selection criterion, involves $2^K$ logical classes, and existing approximations to it suffer from a non-convergence error floor or a shielding effect. We introduce a decoder-agnostic post-selection strategy for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, called parity push post-selection (PPPS), which re-decodes a shot once per logical observable with a push toward the opposite parity. Each push adds one check node and one variable node to the Tanner graph of the detector error model, and we accept a shot only when every re-decoding returns a solution in the original logical class. We show that, with degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding, PPPS accepts a shot exactly when the logical gap exceeds the push strength $\lambda$. Applied with the Relay-BP decoder to the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code at $p=10^{-3}$ and the [[144,12,12]] code at $p=3\times10^{-3}$ under circuit-level depolarizing noise, PPPS lowers the logical error rate by factors of about 50 and 75, respectively, at rejection rates near 1%. We observe that PPPS rejects failures that prior post-selection strategies cannot reject, and thus shows improved performance.

authors.name: Hong Jun Kim, Gun Sik Min, Seok-Hyung Lee, Jun Heo

papers.title: Addressable transversal CCZ gates on almost good quantum LDPC codes and nearly optimal magic state protocols
papers.summary: Assuming uniform subfield product expansion, we construct quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes with distances $\Omega_\epsilon(N/\log^2N)$ and at least $N^{1-\epsilon}$ individually addressable logical CCZ gates on pairwise disjoint triples of logical qubits, for every fixed $0<\epsilon<1$. With all logical qubits outside these triples initialized to $|0\rangle$, any subset of the corresponding logical CCZ gates can be implemented with a transversal physical CCZ circuit. As applications, we obtain two nearly optimal magic state protocols: CCZ distillation with arbitrarily small overhead exponent $\gamma \rightarrow 0$ and error suppression of nearly linear order, and a magic state fountain that directly prepares $N^{1-\epsilon}$ encoded CCZ magic states with nearly linear distance $\Omega_\epsilon(N/\log^2N)$. The construction uses balanced products of expanding graph covers. The assumption concerns Reed--Solomon codes on three subfields of characteristic two and pairwise coprime extension degrees, a local hypothesis studied in a companion manuscript. We design the expanding graph covers to admit many common classical codewords, which yield logical operators whose pairings select the logical CCZ gates independently. Without the product expansion assumption, the graph covers also yield classical LDPC codes over a fixed field with almost linear dimension and linear distance that satisfy a multiplication property: the coordinatewise product of any three codewords lies in a second LDPC code of linear distance.

authors.name: Shi Jie Samuel Tan, Guanyu Zhu

papers.title: Subsystem evolution in the history state formalism
papers.summary: We present a relational framework for characterizing the evolution of quantum composite systems, based on the correlations within a history state describing the whole evolution relative to a quantum reference clock. While total system-clock entanglement entropy consistently measures the unitary evolution of the closed global system, a different picture emerges for the reduced state of an open subsystem, whose evolution is generally non-unitary due to environmental coupling. We introduce a general formalism that quantifies open-subsystem dynamics using a subsystem-clock mutual information derived from the history state. We demonstrate that this quantity serves as a consistent quantifier of subsystem evolution with respect to a given clock basis, can be applied to arbitrary dynamics, and reduces to system-time entanglement entropy in the global limit. Furthermore, maximizing this measure over all clock bases yields a basis-independent bound on the maximum evolution achievable relative to the clock, directly linked to the difference between the subsystem's entanglement with the rest of the history state and its entanglement with the environment. Finally, we derive analytical expressions for qubit clocks, illustrate our results using spin 1/2 and spin 1 quantum walks, and present a full matrix formalism of Kraus operators for describing the most general subsystem evolution.

authors.name: A. Boette, F. Lomoc, N. Canosa, R. Rossignoli

papers.title: QWeaver: Quantum Circuit Cut Workflow with MLIR-based Compiler, Runtime, and Weaver Hybrid Tasks
papers.summary: Quantum computers available today are constrained by limited qubit counts and high noise levels, making the direct execution of large quantum circuits infeasible on a single device, and while quantum circuit cutting addresses this by partitioning a large circuit into smaller subcircuits for independent execution, orchestrating the full end-to-end workflow remains a significant programming challenge. In this paper, we present QWeaver, a task-graph-based programming and orchestration workflow framework for quantum circuit cutting that accepts OpenQASM quantum circuits as input and constructs a directed acyclic task graph. In this graph, the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR)-based circuit cut is the first task, responsible for analyzing and partitioning the input circuit into executable fragment representations; the generated fragments are then handed to a set of quantum circuit execution tasks that depend on the cut task and can be dispatched concurrently across available quantum backends via the Quantum Intelligent Runtime System (Q-IRIS). Finally, a weaving task, dependent on all execution tasks, performs classical post-processing that applies quasi-probability reconstruction techniques to combine the sampled measurement outcomes of all fragments and recover an accurate approximation of the original circuit's output distribution. We describe the architecture of QWeaver, its integration with Q-IRIS and the execution engine for the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR-EE), validate end-to-end reconstruction on GHZ and Harris-Ross instances, and evaluate systems and width trade-offs on structured GHZ simulator workloads.

authors.name: Narasinga Rao Miniskar, Elaine Wong, Vicente Leyton-Ortega, Sharmin Afrose, Jeffrey S. Vetter, Travis S. Humble

papers.title: Spectral Engineering of Charge Localization and Work Reliability in Collective Quantum Batteries
papers.summary: The performance of a quantum battery depends not only on how much energy it stores, but also on how rapidly useful charge can be restored after work extraction. We show how engineering the reservoir spectrum connects these properties in an interacting collective-spin battery. Interactions separate the Dicke transition frequencies, allowing frequency-selective pumping and loss to control where excitation accumulates and how populations move along the ladder. Analytical results relate the pump-to-loss ratio to charge localization, fluctuations, and extractable work. Two reservoirs producing the same mean charge can nevertheless exhibit markedly different localization and charging times. Under repeated extraction, finite-time recharging also generates correlations between successive work outputs. At matched mean work, these correlations can reverse the ordering of single-cycle and long-time fluctuations: a protocol with larger fluctuations in individual strokes can deliver more reliable accumulated work. An exact counting relation connects these statistics to net charging-energy transfer, while relaxation modes distinguish recovery of the stationary state from recovery of useful work. Finally, local dephasing redistributes population among collective-spin sectors, leading to an exact stationary symmetry-dilution law and a finite operating window for work extraction under a collective transverse controller.

authors.name: He-Guang Xu, G. D. de Moraes Neto

papers.title: Stationary Quantum Time Series: Spectral Theory of Process Memory and Measurement Records
papers.summary: Classical time series analysis converts temporal dependence into structure that can be learned from a single observed trajectory, through stationarity, ergodicity, spectral representation, and finite-memory models. Quantum experiments are naturally time series: every run is a sequence of interventions and outcomes, and the memory of an open system is written in its temporal statistics. However, the classical foundation cannot be translated directly: measuring a process and forgetting the outcome differs from not measuring at all, so no single family of joint probability distributions describes a quantum process. We develop a process-tensor framework for stationary quantum time series and establish its first structural theorems. For stationary combs of finite quantum Markov order l relative to a fixed informationally complete causal break, we construct a finite-dimensional causal transfer map of dimension at most d^{4l}, where d bounds the system Hilbert-space dimension at each step. ... These results supply the stationary foundation on which quantum spectral analysis, model identification, and single-trajectory inference can be built.

authors.name: Hai Wang

papers.title: Covering the Pauli Observables: Sampling Thresholds and the Design Effect of a Measurement Setting
papers.summary: Quantum state tomography and shadow-based estimation rely on measuring Pauli observables. An experiment does not measure them one at a time: it chooses a measurement setting that assigns one of the bases X, Y or Z to each qubit, and a single run in that setting yields estimates of every Pauli observable compatible with it. We say that the setting covers those observables. We determine how many random settings cover a prescribed fraction of all Pauli observables. As the number of settings grows exponentially with the number of qubits, the covered fraction has a sharp threshold at a growth rate of $3^{3/4}$ per qubit, set by the rate-distortion function of covering at zero distortion. We give an explicit expression for the number of settings needed to reach a target fraction, accurate up to a remainder that reduces to a small oscillation for many qubits, and show that random sampling is asymptotically optimal up to a factor of less than 1.69. Coverage does not determine what a setting contributes to an estimator. Observables covered by one setting are estimated from the same outcomes, so their estimates are correlated. We quantify this correlation through the design effect of a setting, which equals the squared Pauli expectation that the setting captures and depends on the target state. We derive its mean over settings in closed form for every state and show that it can be estimated without bias from the measurement data. In simulations on six qubits, measuring settings needs 7.6 to 38 times fewer circuit runs than measuring the same number of observables independently. At high coverage, fitting the outcome histograms instead of averaged estimates roughly halves the reconstruction error, mainly because the fit counts how many settings cover each observable. The correlation itself costs such a fit about a factor of two, and a larger design effect signals more to gain from modeling it.

authors.name: Kausthubh Chandramouli, Noah Siekierski, Bojko N. Bakalov, Dror Baron

papers.title: Aharonov-Bohm blockade of complete reversal in coupled Rabi cavities
papers.summary: When a common bias reverses two bistable fields, the system can pass through either of two single-reversal configurations on its way to the favored state. We show that interference between these two orders of reversal can block the final step. In a dimer of coupled quantum Rabi cavities, the four field configurations form a loop, and a complex photon-hopping amplitude threads it with an Aharonov-Bohm flux. Near half a flux quantum, the two paths to complete reversal interfere destructively: in microscopic simulations, a slow uniform sweep reverses one field with probability 0.998, although the final bias favors reversing both. A four-state model calibrated at zero bias predicts how the window of this Aharonov-Bohm blockade narrows with sweep time. The blocked state remains coherent. A differential pulse followed by a return sweep converts the relative phase of the two single-reversal configurations into a fringe in the joint field signs, with contrast 0.95. In a trimer, a phase gradient imprinted between sweeps determines whether the next sweep adds or removes a reversed field: reversing the second of two gradients changes the most probable outcome from three reversed fields to one.

authors.name: Shu He, Liwei Duan

papers.title: Imaging chiral snake states in a qubit array with programmable gauge fields
papers.summary: Spatially varying magnetic fields steer charged particles along directed paths. Where a field reverses sign, particles follow snake-like orbits along the reversal line, in a direction set by both the field orientation and the sign of their energy. Transport measurements have detected such snake states, but imaging their dynamics in a reprogrammable field landscape remains challenging. Here we digitally simulate the Harper--Hofstadter model with programmable synthetic magnetic fields on a 49-qubit superconducting processor. In each Trotter step, every hopping term is one native fractional-iSWAP gate, and single-qubit $Z$ rotations set all 36 plaquette fluxes independently, without additional entangling gates. Uniform, random, and stepped flux landscapes reveal Aharonov--Bohm suppression of diagonal propagation, disorder-induced slowing, and magnetic reflection. At a field reversal, bonding and antibonding initial states, which carry opposite energy biases, propagate in opposite directions, and both directions reverse when the field is inverted. A symmetry analysis of these reversals yields a chiral displacement of nearly one lattice spacing after ten Trotter rounds, with symmetry-breaking residuals below 0.05 lattice spacings. Bond-resolved flux programming with site-resolved imaging thus provides a quantitative tool for synthetic gauge fields and a route to time-dependent gauge fields and interacting particles.

authors.name: Hanyi Wang, Lijun Sun, Bihao Guo, Weizhi Tao, Jian Ding, Shengbin Wang, Xinfang Zhang, Wei-Yong Zhang, Hantao Sun

papers.title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control
papers.summary: Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with $n$ physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/\epsilon)$ logical qubits, where $\epsilon$ is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/\epsilon)$; an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to ${\sf polylog}(n/\epsilon)$.

authors.name: Christopher A. Pattison, Jeongwan Haah, John Preskill

papers.title: Faster than square-root run-time in adiabatic quantum algorithms for Exact Cover 3
papers.summary: By intertwining ideas from sequential and adiabatic quantum computing, we propose a quantum algorithm for the problem class Exact Cover 3, which is a sub-class of 3-satisfiability (3-SAT) problems and NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) complete. We find a quantum run-time which is significantly faster than the square-root run-time $N\to N^{1/2}$ of the Grover algorithm. Depending on the structure of the problem (e.g., connectivity of clauses), the run-time scaling may range from approximately third root $N\to N^{1/3}$ to nearly fourth root $N\to N^{1/4}$, possibly even faster.

authors.name: Gernot Schaller, Ralf Sch\"utzhold

papers.title: Analysis of a Homodyne-Like Measurement Scheme Using Photon Counters and Weak Local Oscillator
papers.summary: In standard homodyne detection, an unknown optical signal state is combined with a local oscillator (LO) at a beam splitter (BS), and the appropriately integrated intensities at the two outputs of the BS are subtracted to obtain an approximate quadrature measurement. Accurate quadrature measurements require a high-amplitude LO and high-efficiency detectors. By varying the LO phase, the optical state in the mode matching the LO can be reconstructed. In many practical settings, a high-intensity LO is not desirable, which has led to the exploration of homodyne-like measurement schemes that replace photodiodes with photon-counting detectors and use an LO with a low average photon number. In this paper, we investigate what features of the unknown state can be determined by counting the total-photon number in one or both outgoing paths after the BS, keeping the mode of the LO fixed but adjusting its phase and magnitude. We find that it is possible to determine the unknown optical state in the mode matching the LO conditional on the number of photons in the orthogonal modes on the same path. If both the phase and the intensity of the LO can be varied, the statistics of just one of the detectors is sufficient to infer these parameters, but both detectors are required when the LO has a fixed intensity. Our analysis is carried out in the infinite-data limit, assuming access to the full photon-number distribution from one or both detectors.

authors.name: Arik Avagyan, Emanuel Knill, Scott Glancy

papers.title: Topological Origin of Directional Amplification in Arbitrary-Dimensional Non-Hermitian Lattices
papers.summary: In non-Hermitian lattices, combinations of gain, loss and nonreciprocal couplings can generate exponentially growing directional amplification with applications in signal processing and precision measurement. An intriguing question is whether such amplification has a universal topological origin in arbitrary dimensions. Here we establish a dimension-independent framework to uncover the topological origin of directional amplification based on the concept of amoeba, which is the logarithmic image of the singularities of the response generating function. The complement of the amoeba in the logarithmic parameter space consists of connected components, each carrying a distinct and discrete topological label. We show that the asymptotic response is governed by the component extending toward negative infinity. When the origin of the logarithmic parameter space is outside this component and not on its boundary, there must exist some directions in which the response is exponentially amplified. Otherwise, there is no directional amplification in any direction. Our results provide a general topological criterion for classifying the responses in arbitrary-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices.

authors.name: Zhenxiang Wu, Linfeng Zhang, Haitan Xu

papers.title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
papers.summary: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

authors.name: Zhi-Lei Zhang, Lianxiang Cui, C. P. Sun, Kohei Nakajima, Kazuyuki Aihara

papers.title: Distinguishing Conserved Quantum Sectors via Measurement Record Features
papers.summary: Conservation laws partition the Hilbert space of a quantum system into invariant sectors that are often difficult to identify directly. Repeated measurements on an ancillary probe, however, generate a measurement record that provides information about the occupied sector. Here we develop a framework for identifying conserved sectors using a $(K+1)$-dimensional feature vector of record statistics, comprising the average outcome frequency and pair-outcome correlations up to $K$ measurement cycles apart. For fixed $K$, the feature vector can be evaluated at a cost linear in record length. In quantum non-demolition measurement models, the average outcome frequency suffices for accurate sector identification. For an interacting spin bath with nontrivial dynamics within each sector, incorporating temporal correlations between successive and more widely separated measurements into the record feature vector substantially improves classification fidelity. Our framework provides an efficient approach to conserved-sector identification and demonstrates the importance of temporal correlations in distinguishing the underlying sector dynamics.

authors.name: Hao Zhu, Guo-Feng Zhang, Wen-Long Ma

papers.title: Vanilla Adiabatic Quantum Optimization Can Have Subexponential Advantage
papers.summary: We construct a family of objective functions $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ for which vanilla adiabatic quantum optimization along $H(s) = -(1-s)\sum_{i=1}^n X_i + s\sum_x f(x)\lvert x\rangle\!\langle x\rvert$ finds the global minimizer in $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time, whereas any classical algorithm requires $\exp(n^{\Omega(1)})$ time to do so in the black-box model. Our result is achieved by replacing the linearization technique in an earlier work of Leng et al. (arXiv:2504.14841), which establishes a similar subexponential quantum speedup using a transverse field Ising mixer rather than $-\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$.

authors.name: Yufan Zheng

papers.title: Accelerating Quantum Error Correction Simulations under Coherent Noise with Compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product States
papers.summary: Reliable assessment of quantum error correction requires understanding how coherent errors affect logical performance. Although tensor networks naturally capture coherent interference, entanglement growth and large qubit counts make repeated sampling costly. Here we develop a compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product State (CAMPS) framework that reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles qubits released by measurements, evolves a compressed residual state, and accelerates sampling through rotation fusion and compilation tailored to the MPS layout. Surface-code benchmarks under fixed-sign coherent noise yield accurate logical error estimates at small bond dimensions, while random-sign simulations up to distance $d=9$ and on the $[[72,12,6]]$ bivariate bicycle code match the Pauli-twirling approximation results. Compared with uncompiled CAMPS, compiled CAMPS converges at smaller bond dimensions and achieves order-of-magnitude sampling speedups at equal bond dimension, opening a scalable route to studying coherent error propagation in larger fault-tolerant circuits.

authors.name: Jiale Huang, Yaojian Chen, Ke Liu, Dingshun Lv, Mingpu Qin

papers.title: Odd-Even Effects on Liouvillian Spectra and Relaxation Dynamics in Boundary-Driven Spin Chains
papers.summary: We investigate odd-even effects on Liouvillian spectra and relaxation dynamics in boundary-driven XY and cluster chains. With the bulk couplings and boundary dissipation rule fixed, the parity of chain length determines whether non-decaying oscillatory modes exist. Consequently, odd- and even-sized chains exhibit qualitatively different dynamical behaviors. We trace this mechanism to the coupling between bulk Majorana paths and the boundary jump operators. An isolated path supports undamped modes, and products of an even number of its Majorana operators span a non?decaying subspace of even operators. This structure yields nonzero purely imaginary eigenvalues of the Liouvillian and persistent contributions to bond correlations or magnetization after preparation in product states. The mechanism extends to cluster interactions of even range under a fixed boundary dissipation rule. The existence and frequencies of the persistent modes are independent of the magnitudes of the positive boundary dissipation rates. Our results unveil how chain parity controls the existence of persistent dynamics.

authors.name: Zhen-Yu Zheng, Shu Chen

papers.title: Reliability of quantum communication over erasure channels
papers.summary: Quantum information can be reliably transmitted at rates below the quantum capacity with an error that vanishes as the number of channel uses grows. The reliability function characterizes the optimal exponential decay rate of this error. For quantum erasure channels with a prime input dimension, we determine the reliability function exactly at all positive communication rates below capacity that meet or exceed an explicit critical rate. Notably, stabilizer coding strategies attain this optimal reliability throughout this regime.

authors.name: Hongyu Mao, Kun Fang

papers.title: CCZ gate beyond the strong Rydberg-blockade regime
papers.summary: We present a protocol for implementing a controlled-controlled-Z (CCZ) gate on a neutral-atom platform, employing three individually addressable atoms confined in a linear array of optical tweezers and operating under finite Rydberg-Rydberg interaction (RRI). The protocol combines successive excitation of the Rydberg atoms with analytically determined pulses and uses two Rydberg levels to access opposite-sign interaction shifts. We show two different paths to get the conditional phase in the target atom: a pair of target pulses with opposite phases and a single detuned target pulse followed by a local phase correction. We derive analytical expressions for the time-integrated Rydberg populations to calculate the associated decay errors and also evaluate gate performance through master-equation simulations. Numerical comparisons with a fast Rydberg-antiblockade (RAB)-based CCZ protocol show improved gate performance at larger interatomic separations within the parameter regime considered. Monte Carlo sampling further quantifies the sensitivity to thermally induced position fluctuations. These results identify the tradeoffs between gate duration, Rydberg-state exposure, and interaction sensitivity, providing an analytically specified route to native three-qubit phase gates beyond the strong-blockade regime.

authors.name: Snigdhadev Ray, Sinchan Snigdha Rej

papers.title: Quantum Parallel Algorithm for Multivariate Trace Estimation with Applications
papers.summary: Estimating multivariate traces Tr(A1A2......Ak) is a fundamental task arising across diverse fields. In this paper, We develop a quantum algorithm for this problem tailored to near-term quantum devices. We access matrices by preparing their vectorized states. This access mode yields a tensor-network representation of the multivariate trace, which in turn guides the design of a parallel algorithm. The resulting circuit has depth dominated solely by that of the input oracle and independent of the number of matrices k, at the cost of a qubit count scaling as {\Theta}(k)-a trade-off between circuit depth and circuit size. Moreover, the circuit exhibits a simple modular structure that allows explicit distribution over O(k) devices. We further establish efficient preparation circuits for a broad range of matrix classes, demonstrating the wide applicability of our approach. we present two applications: spectral sum estimation and a quantum implementation of the classical Lanczos method. Both reduce the target problem to sums of multivariate traces, thereby avoiding the construction of matrix polynomial transformations and achieving two levels of parallelism. For certain matrix classes, the resulting algorithms reduce circuit depth by a factor equal to the degree of the approximating polynomial. The shallow circuit depth and distributed implementation make our algorithms particularly suitable for near-term devices.

authors.name: Honghong Lin, Yun Shang

papers.title: Gradient Blindness in Adaptive Architecture Search for IQP Born Machines
papers.summary: Instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP) Born machines learn a probability distribution from data with a circuit of commuting gates that a classical computer trains at hundreds of qubits. Adaptive algorithms grow a sparse circuit from a small seed by adding in every round the candidate gates with the largest loss gradient. Such algorithms never add a candidate whose gradient vanishes, so the choice of seed decides which circuits they can reach. Here we show that a candidate gate has a nonzero gradient for some angles of the circuit exactly when its generator is the sum of an odd number of linearly independent generators already in the circuit. The common seed of one-qubit gates therefore never adds a gate on an even number of qubits, which exact gradients on 12 qubits confirm. A seed of one-qubit gates plus the edges of the Chow-Liu tree sees every candidate, and its circuits match the full circuits on 12 and 16 qubits with 10 to 13 percent of their parameters. At 484 qubits, a heredity pool keeps the search over higher-order gates feasible, and the circuits grown from this seed reach a lower test loss than the dense two-body circuit with 6 percent of its parameters, although the higher-order gates add no gain.

authors.name: Sebastian W\"olckert, Gerhard Stenzel, Michael Poppel, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien, Jonas Stein

papers.title: Quantifying extractable imaginarity with qubit triangles
papers.summary: Two qubit states with the same robustness of imaginarity can differ in the robustness attainable by real filtering on a successful outcome. We represent the input robustness $R$ and the largest conditional robustness $\kappa$ by the base of a right triangle and the slope of its hypotenuse, respectively. Twice the area, $R^2\kappa$, defines a faithful, convex measure that is monotone on average under real instruments. In arbitrary finite dimensions, maximizing the mean normalized area of the extracted qubits gives the pointwise smallest strongly monotone extension of the qubit measure. We derive computable bounds on this area by determining the maximum mean squared robustness of the output qubits. This maximum equals the Bures quantum $\chi^2$ divergence between the input and its real part. A projection onto orthogonal real subspaces attains the maximum and, when its outcome is retained, preserves the quantum Fisher information at the midpoint of a mixture of the input and its complex conjugate. We obtain exact areas for states with commuting real and imaginary parts and for pure states mixed with white noise. Two eight-dimensional states have identical $R$, $\kappa$, and optimal mean squared robustness, yet their different areas rule out deterministic conversion by real operations in one direction.

authors.name: Meng-Li Guo, Chen-Xin Xu, Wen Xu, Shao-Ming Fei

papers.title: A Convex-Roof Affinity-Square Measure of Quantum Imaginarity
papers.summary: Quantum imaginarity characterizes the part of a quantum state that cannot be represented by real density matrices in a fixed reference basis. We study an affinity-square measure of imaginarity for pure states and its convex-roof extension to mixed states. The pure state quantity is defined by minimizing the affinity-square measure over the convex set of real states. This optimization admits a closed expression determined by the modulus of the conjugation overlap between a state and its complex conjugate. The measure vanishes precisely when the state is real up to a global phase. We prove that the convex-roof extension is faithful, convex, monotone under real operations, and nonincreasing on average under selective real operations. For arbitrary single-qubit mixed states, we evaluate the convex roof exactly and express it in terms of the imaginary component of the off-diagonal density-matrix element. We also compare pure-state imaginarity with an auxiliary affinity-square coherence functional and give the corresponding phase weights.

authors.name: Nan-Nan Guan, Meng-Li Guo, Xue-Na Zhu, Zhi-Xiang Jin, Yan-Hui Zhou

papers.title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
